author: macruzbar
text:
### Information for newbies
**New to machine learning and data science?** No question is too basic or too simple. Feel free to start your own thread, or use this thread as a place to post any first-timer clarifying questions for the Kaggle community to help you with!

**New to Kaggle?** Take a look at a few videos to learn a bit more about [site etiquette](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aIus8si_Et0), [Kaggle lingo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sEJHyuWKd-s), and [how to enter a competition using Kaggle Notebooks](https://www.youtube.com/watch?&v=GJBOMWpLpTQ). Publish and share your [models on Kaggle Models](https://www.kaggle.com/docs/models#publishing-a-model)!

**Looking for a team?** Express your interest in joining a team through our [Team Up](https://www.kaggle.com/discussions/product-feedback/341195) feature.

**Remember**: Kaggle is for everyone. Whether you're teaming up or sharing tips in the competition forum, we expect everyone to follow our Kaggle community guidelines.

### Competition's Official Discord
In addition to this competition forum, you can continue the discussion in our official Kaggle Discord Server here:
# [discord.gg/kaggle](http://discord.gg/kaggle)
 
The Discord is a great place to ask getting started questions, chat about the nuances of this competition, and connect with potential team mates. Learn more about Discord at our [announcement here](https://www.kaggle.com/discussions/general/429933). Here are a few things to keep in mind though:

**1. Discord Competition Channels are 'Public' - Don't Share Private Information**

Discord channels for specific competitions are considered 'public' spaces where you are allowed to talk about competition details. Please remember that private sharing of competition code or data outside of your team is, as always, not permitted. Code sharing must always be done publicly through the Kaggle forums/notebooks.

**2. Discord Competition Channels are Not Monitored by Staff - Keep Important Information on the Kaggle Forums**

Kaggle Staff and Hosts running competitions will not monitor Discord or be available to answer questions in Discord. This is intended to be a more casual space to discuss competitions and help each other. Please keep important questions, insights, writeups, and other valuable conversation on the Kaggle forums. 

Happy modeling!

title: Before Solving ARC, Should We Redefine the Problem Itself?
author: kevinnqt
text:
I’ve been thinking about ARC-style tasks from a slightly different angle.

Most approaches seem to focus on pattern recognition, transformation rules, or model scaling. But I’m starting to wonder if we might be missing a more fundamental question:

What exactly do we mean by “intelligence” in this context?

If we look at these tasks from an agent perspective, intelligence might not just be about finding the correct transformation. It could also involve:

Allocating limited resources (time, compute, steps) efficiently
Avoiding unnecessary or high-risk operations
Recognizing when a current strategy is insufficient
Knowing when to explore vs exploit

In that sense, “being intelligent” might be less about being correct immediately, and more about how the system navigates uncertainty and constraints over time.

This raises a few questions I’d love to hear thoughts on:

Should ARC be treated as a static mapping problem, or as a sequential decision process?
How important is internal state representation compared to raw input-output matching?
Do current approaches sufficiently model uncertainty and failure modes?
Could a smaller system with better structure outperform larger models on these tasks?

Curious how others here are thinking about this - especially from a systems or agent design perspective.

title: Before Solving ARC, Should We Redefine the Problem Itself?
author: heirloomseed
text: I think that it is important to note that since humans can solve these problems directly without terrible effort we should focus a bit on why? I have long thought that domain knowledge in the form of previous human experience plays a key role (somewhat obvious). In many ways this is a challenge to see how actionable human-like experience can be transferred to the realm of AI efficiently. This is a surprisingly tricky problem. We try to approximate this experience with simple heuristics that make sense to us with respect to the problem domain but it is very difficult to truly recreate the "active" experiential knowledge that humans possess. What seems simple to us belies years of actual experience that we cannot fully consciously inspect. I think that a good world model coupled with a suitable agent framework and some clever heuristics could make great progress on this challenge.

title: Before Solving ARC, Should We Redefine the Problem Itself?
author: rakibul1410
text:
I believe this is primarily a mapping problem. The model needs to predict potential future outcomes, similar to how humans consider their options before making a decision. By observing a situation, humans can often determine that taking a specific path, such as going right, may take less time. From my understanding, no existing architecture can adequately address this issue on its own. We need to redesign the system by integrating agentic behavior into the architecture. Currently, relying solely on foundational models and tools is not sufficient, in my opinion. I believe that a smaller model with a very structured architecture could potentially solve this problem entirely.
This competition might reshape the future of LLMs

title: Before Solving ARC, Should We Redefine the Problem Itself?
author: aidetective
text:
I don't believe ARC-3 is a good test for AGI. In this sense:
All the puzzles rely on simple recognition of the problem + planning.

They don't involve having to have any "flash of insight". More like "flash of recognition". ARC-3 is more like "puzzle recognition".

e.g. the one with the water is just recognising having seen pixel water simulations before and recognising symbolic representation of cups.

That's all well and good but consider someone trying the "sliding-15" puzzle for the first time, this is more like AGI since we first explore moving about the tiles, then we formulate little theories about how to get each piece in place, and invent strategies.

I think the ARC-3 puzzles are too simple for real AGI. It is a small step in the right direction. Real AGI should be more focussed on the solving complicated tasks than the recognition IMO. I would prefer a blind genius AGI than a dumb seeing AI.

TLDR: An AI that can play chess well is better than an AI that can just recognise the game is called Chess.

title: Before Solving ARC, Should We Redefine the Problem Itself?
author: yuriao
text: I think whether ARC is a mapping or sequential decision process depending on how much prior knowledge is already present in the agent's memory system. An navie (totally untrained) agent in the ARC games does not know why they are here, and what they expect, so at least in the first few each steps they will need to do decision->outcome->refine cognitive map -> next decision (sequential decision style). An expert agent, which have large amount of relevant knowledge, will directly recognize the step's place in its memory and find its corresponding next state, i.e. a mapping operation (o(1) in the most optimal case). However, I think when build a naive agent, if the structure design can reflect the mechanism of the game, i.e. the structure is prior knowledge, this could help the naive agent do one-shot or few-shot learning of the task

title: Before Solving ARC, Should We Redefine the Problem Itself?
author: jacquelynnhall
text:
I posted kind of a book to a different thread, so I won't repeat all of it: [here](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/arc-prize-2026-arc-agi-3/discussion/688114#3436711) (in case you're curious).

But the TL;DR version (...comparatively :D) is that the hypothesis I've been working from is that the problem space (maybe/probably) requires managing information appropriateness, storage, and application of new learnings to help models compensate for not having a lifetime of playing games under their metaphorical belts.

The scoring makes it resource constrained, but my framing had been more along the lines of: when I play a game, what am I taking for granted? What do -I- need to play well, and how can I translate that... in a generalized way, of course (to avoid targeting specific mechanics and stuff)? How much information is too much information? 

In fact, my very first attempt (not submitted--unsure whether I'm going to join the competition, but it's an interesting space to explore), I tried out this hypothesis: "Could a smaller system with better structure outperform larger models on these tasks?"

The smallest models I tried needed so much handholding to produce anything remotely useful that I concluded it was going to be more effort than I had patience to make them primary. Think: encoding the scientific method into strict stages because I needed them to do better at reasoning than they had the capacity for. 

I'm experimenting with the size and type of models still, and I genuinely don't know whether my approach will work, which is part of the fun. But it's the framing I've gone with because I'm a systems person, and that's my jam. :) 

Good luck!

title: What does 0.25 on LB mean?
author: sergeifironov
text:
How Scoring Works

​
Per-Level Scoring

For each level the AI completes, calculate:
level_score = (human_baseline_actions / ai_actions) ^ 2
If human baseline is 10 actions and AI takes 10 → level score is 1.0 (100%)
If human baseline is 10 actions and AI takes 20 → level score is 0.25 (50%)
If human baseline is 10 actions and AI takes 1,00 → level score is 0.01 (1%)
​

Per-Level Score Cap

The maximum score per level is capped at 1.0x human baseline. If an AI discovers a shortcut and completes a level faster than humans, it still only receives 1.0.
This encourages building AI that generalizes across games rather than exploiting individual levels.
​

Per-Game Aggregation

The game score is the weighted average of all per-level scores, using a 1 index of the level as the weight, for that game.
Example: A game has 7 levels. The AI scores:
Levels 1-3: 0.25 each (took twice as many actions as human)
Levels 4-7: 0 each (did not complete the level)
Game score = (0.25x1 + 0.25x2 + 0.5x3 + 0x4 + 0x5 + 0x6 + 0x7) / (1+2+3+4+5+6+7) = 0.01289 (1.29%)
Per-level weighted average underweights the starting levels which are tutorial/easy levels and overweights the more difficult levels where mastery must be demonstrated.


Total score is the average of all game scores

title: Simplified submission framework
author: jeroencottaar
text:
The official notebooks show how to submit your agents to run on ARC-AGI3, but they're pretty complicated. Also, they do nothing if you're not actually submitting - they don't actually run on the 25 training games then.

title: What if AGI isn't about doing everything but about knowing what it can't do?
author: kevinnqt
text:
Participating in ARC-AGI-3 has been one of the more philosophically disorienting experiences I've had in AI development. Not because the benchmark is hard (it is), but because it forced me to question what I thought I understood about intelligence.

Most definitions of AGI I've encountered frame it as capability breadth: a system that can do anything a human can do. I've come to think that's the wrong frame entirely.

From where I stand - drawing on cognitive science, epistemology, and a bit of continental philosophy - AGI is not about maximal capability. It's about the capacity to recognize one's own limits, and from that recognition, find the direction to expand them.

A system that can't fail gracefully, that can't say "I don't have the right frame for this," that can't distinguish between what it knows and what it's pattern-matching toward - that system isn't intelligent. It's just fast.

---

On the IPO problem nobody talks about

I've noticed that most ARC discussions circle around Input → Process → Output. The refinement loop. The architecture. The reasoning chain.

Very rarely do I see anyone seriously address the D that has to precede the : Data.

Not training data in the conventional sense. I mean: where does the *substrate* come from? What is the node pool from which any input draws meaning? If you don't have a structured semantic foundation that a system can anchor concepts to, then your Input isn't really input - it's noise looking for a pattern to land on.

This is actually what ARC-AGI-3 is surfacing, I think. The games don't give you data. They give you *interaction*. And the gap between those two things is where most AI systems fall apart.

Humans don't struggle with LS20 because they have more compute. They don't struggle because they've seen similar games. They succeed because they arrive with a pre-structured world model - a massive, mostly-unconscious graph of named concepts, relations, and frames - and they collapse that graph onto the novel environment almost instantly.

That pre-structure is the data layer. And it's almost entirely absent in current agent architectures.

---

What I'm building alongside this contest

I have a personal AI project running in parallel - Pete - and the repo linked here is specifically the data layer: a ~100k node fractal semantic graph that functions as a cognitive substrate.

The design philosophy came from a simple observation:

In cognitive science, consciousness is often modeled as a *dynamic activation pattern* over a much larger unconscious structure. Attention doesn't create the content it attends to - it selects from what's already there.

So Pete doesn't encode information as vectors. It encodes it as named nodes organized by meaning and frame of reference. The full graph is the unconscious. Active attention is a small, focused subgraph pulled from it based on context.

Same substrate. Different attention pattern. Different frame. Different "persona."

The claim isn't that this produces consciousness. The claim is that without this kind of pre-structured semantic substrate, any input processing is fundamentally impoverished - because the system has no stable ground to anchor new concepts against.

This maps directly to what I see failing in ARC-AGI-3 agents: they process the frame they're given, but they have no deep structure to place it in. No world model to collapse onto the novel environment. No way to recognize that what looks like a rotator here is the same structural role as a switch somewhere else - because they're not tracking Meaning across Name changes.

---

A different question about AGI

I'll leave with the question that's been sitting with me throughout this contest:

If a system can't recognize that its current frame might be wrong - if it can't step back from its own processing and ask "wait, am I even using the right lens here?" - can we really call it intelligent?

Maybe the benchmark for AGI isn't solving every task. Maybe it's the capacity to know when you're at the edge of your current understanding, and do something coherent with that knowledge rather than just failing louder.

Interested to hear how others are thinking about the data substrate problem - and whether the distinction between Input and the pre-structured ground that makes Input meaningful resonates with anyone else here.

Git: https://github.com/jkdkr2439/Pete_Unconscious_Substrate

title: What if AGI isn't about doing everything but about knowing what it can't do?
author: dariocopparoni
text:
As animals, we receive information every day through our senses. Within us, we have the ability to process this sensory data in order to understand the world around us. I believe that from the very beginning, we have the capacity to recognise where this information comes from. For example, if I observe a sheep, my brain is able to understand that the white colour, the shape, and the smell all come from the same object (the sheep).

We also have the ability to generalise. So, if I see another living being with the same or similar characteristics, I can relate it to the one I saw before (the sheep) and say, “That is the same type of object I have already seen.”

We are capable of understanding cause‑and‑effect relationships as well. For instance, if I see a ram charge at a wooden fence and break it, I know that the fence is broken because of the ram’s action. 

Through these observations we gain experience, which we can later use to achieve our purpose. So, if I want to break another section of fencing, I know that one possible method would be to make the ram charge at it.

The point is, why I would do that, maybe it is something necessary to archive something bigger like for example free all animals? What does mean have a goal? 

Another thing to consider is this: if we learn through experience, who teaches a duckling, the moment it hatches, to start following the first moving shape it sees? Or who teaches a baby to suckle as soon as its mouth touches the breast? Clearly, we already have something within us that allows us to take our first steps in the world.

Those are some of my starting points for thinking the software 🙂

title: What if AGI isn't about doing everything but about knowing what it can't do?
author: aidetective
text:
Yes, LLMs while it can give you the probabilities for the most likely next token, doesn't include a confidence score of how likely the token is to lead to a good outcome (such as in the case of an language model, that would be a good reaction to it's output).

Some people have tried to fix this by creating Bayesian models, but I think without much success.

I think confidence levels would mostly have to be acquired in post-training reinforcement learning stage. Although to help it along in the training stage the AI should learn what sources it's information came from (journals/twitter/reddit) and also use that to adjust it's confidence levels. In a dreaming, simulation (self-play) mode, it could probably also acquire confidence predictions, as it learns which moves lead to good outcomes. (Similar to how Alpha-zero works). As it trains to increase it's confidence levels, this should be in some-way equivalent to world-building.

If we consider "confidence" and it's opposite "doubt" as emotions. Then what we are talking about is imbuing the AGI with ruidementary emotions. 

Humans tend to ruminate on things which they have low confidence on. Simulating things over and over in their mind until confidence of the corrected course of action is achieved. Not only that but in an open ended topic like mathematics there will always be places where a human is not confident and this spurs them on to new discoveries.

TLDR. Confidence is all you need.

title: Is Offline BFS "Cheating the Spirit" of ARC-AGI-3?
author: komilparmar
text:
There are some public notebooks recently posted including the current highest scoring one (0.44 LB) using what appears to be an offline BFS solver. i.e. Directly instantiating the game engine classes to exhaustively search state spaces, solving ~12/25 games at near-perfect efficiency without any learning or reasoning.

Technically, this is completely legal. It's not hardcoding solutions; it dynamically searches whatever game it's given. The arc-engine is provided as an offline wheel specifically for agents to use.

But it raises a question worth discussing: **is this the kind of solution ARC is trying to reward?**

The competition's stated goal is to advance toward AGI, specifically, agents that can reason about and adapt to novel interactive environments they've never seen. BFS doesn't reason. It enumerates. It succeeds not because it understands the puzzle, but because the state space is small enough to brute-force.

On the other hand, search has always been part of intelligence. **AlphaZero uses MCTS**. Classical planning systems use BFS. And crucially, BFS fails on roughly half the games (large state spaces, stochastic games, complex interactions). The CNN fallback is still doing real work.

So are these notebooks / solutions an impressive engineering solution to an AI problem, or a clever exploit of a benchmark weakness?

I'm genuinely unsure. Curious what others think, especially whether the organizers intended for direct game class instantiation to be in-scope, or whether future editions of ARC-AGI will sandbox the environment to prevent it.

**Most importantly**, can we be sure that such submissions be removed by the hosts at end of the competition if not earlier, or not?

author: jeroencottaar
text: It's definitely cheating. title: Is Offline BFS "Cheating the Spirit" of ARC-AGI-3?
author: sapr3s
text:
The discussion seems to be based on an incorrect assumption about the scores. People are talking about "submissions being removed", "cheating"..etc

First, let's look at the actual public leaderboard. The current top score is 0.68 – that's 0.68% (seriously, one month after start?), not 44% or anything close to it. If someone could solve 12 **hidden** games, their score would be vastly higher (probably tens of percent). Even the best agent is far from that.

Second, the game engine code for the 25 **public**/training games is provided so that people can run and test their agents **locally**. The hidden test games are not accessible that way – you only get to run your agent through the submission API, not by instantiating the engine classes for unseen levels.

Third, using search algorithms like BFS on the **observed environment** (the current level state) is perfectly legitimate. That's not cheating; it's just one possible strategy. The challenge is to find efficient action sequences under uncertainty, not to ban planning.

text:
No, it's a type of artificial intelligence in search algorithms. It used to be widely used in robots. The human brain also uses a type of search algorithm.
When playing chess, coding or making a difficult life decision, we construct probability trees in our minds. Our predictive scenarios—"If I do this, then that will happen, and then..."—are the biological equivalent of the Monte Carlo Tree Search(MCTS) or branch-and-bound pruning done by algorithms. Our brain constantly searches a space of action and selects the situation with the highest reward potential (or the lowest error rate).

Tackling ARC-AGI 3: Leveraging Puzzle Games to Address Data Scarcity
author: yuanwangzhang
text:
# Tackling ARC-AGI 3: Leveraging Puzzle Games to Address Data Scarcity

## Introduction

I'd like to share some preliminary thoughts on approaching ARC-AGI 3 challenges and addressing the critical data scarcity problem. These ideas haven't been rigorously validated through experiments yet, so I'm eager to hear your insights and alternative approaches.

## The Core Challenge: Data Scarcity

The fundamental bottleneck in ARC-AGI 3 is the lack of sufficient training data. While we need diverse reasoning examples, generating high-quality data remains extremely challenging:

- **Manual synthesis**: Doesn't scale well and incurs prohibitive costs that competition prizes may not cover
- **LLM-based synthesis**: Struggles to maintain logical consistency, completeness, and the intricate elegance required for ARC-AGI-style problems

## A Potential Solution: Puzzle + Knowledge-Lock Games

Many modern games follow a "puzzle + knowledge-lock" paradigm that shares structural similarities with ARC-AGI tasks. These games could serve as a rich training data source. I've compiled an extensive list of such games (see appendix below).

## Proposed Approach

### 1. Visual Reasoning Model (Preferred Direction)

I'm inclined toward training a **vision-based reasoning model** rather than a text-based one, for several reasons:

- **GUI Agent parallels**: We can leverage substantial research from GUI agent domains, which share similarities with ARC-AGI's visual nature
- **Feature preservation**: Text-based models may struggle to capture subtle visual patterns and spatial relationships that are crucial for ARC-AGI tasks
- **Direct perception**: Visual models can directly observe grid transformations without lossy text encoding

### 2. Training Strategy

Drawing inspiration from recent work:

- **[MiroThinker](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15726)-style single-step logic**: Focus on atomic reasoning capabilities rather than end-to-end solutions
- **[EvoCUA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.15876)-inspired DPO training**: Train on critical error steps using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) rather than GRPO
  - Target: Key incorrect reasoning steps
  - Advantage: More efficient than training on final answer correctness alone
  - Rationale: Pinpointing where reasoning breaks down yields stronger learning signals

### 3. Data Utilization Strategy

**Challenge**: How to effectively leverage puzzle game data remains an open question.

**Considerations**:
- Training solely on puzzle games will create distributional shift from ARC-AGI
- However, such models may have **greater potential** and **faster adaptation** to ARC-AGI tasks
- The broader reasoning capabilities learned from diverse puzzles could generalize better than narrow ARC-AGI-specific training

**Hybrid approach** (tentative):
1. Pre-train on diverse puzzle game data to build general reasoning capabilities
2. Fine-tune on ARC-AGI-like synthetic problems to align distribution
3. Balance between generalization (puzzle games) and specialization (ARC-AGI synthesis)

## Open Questions

I'm still working through several critical questions:

1. **Data extraction**: What's the optimal way to convert gameplay into training data?
2. **Task alignment**: How do we bridge the gap between game mechanics and ARC-AGI's abstract reasoning?
3. **Synthesis balance**: What ratio of game data to ARC-AGI-like synthetic data yields the best results?
4. **Evaluation**: How do we measure whether puzzle game training actually transfers to ARC-AGI performance?

## Discussion Points

I'd love to hear your thoughts on:

- Has anyone experimented with similar cross-domain transfer approaches?
- Are there better data sources I'm overlooking?
- What are the potential pitfalls of the puzzle game training approach?

title: Tackling ARC-AGI 3: Leveraging Puzzle Games to Address Data Scarcity
author: jacquelynnhall
text:
I've never built anything like this before, so take my thoughts in that context. :) 

Your game list reads like a more and less complete library of my games between Xbox, PlayStation, and Steam. 

I can't speak for all of them, but having beaten many of them (without a walkthrough for some!), I'd say they are way, way more complicated data sources than the goal requires, and possibly to a detriment.

The ARC-AGI-3 site with the games features some replays of the SOTA models doing their best and failing in entertainingly predictable ways. I'm not making fun of the models. They really aren't dumb. 

In my view, they weren't given enough of the right information to do the tasks. They seemed to have minimal prompting (though I can't be sure), so they did what fit the pattern best... which might be one of the worst ways to approach a novel game. You basically should assume you don't know anything except what the game will tell you over time as you do things.  

I'd recommend watching the output along with the actions for some of them, if you get a chance. Not all of them include reasoning, but the Opus and Gemini runs tended to. 

The "fit the pattern best" thing is one of my cautions: an immediate problem many of them had was concluding "this looks like Sokoban!" or "I'm trying to shoot at target with a cannon and make the hit point bar go away!" 

There was no cannon, and the 'hit point' bar was a move counter--expending it lost a life or the level. 

So, while you need a sense of things that -can- happen (ex. when I moved a piece to this interesting looking spot, a thing happened), having a lot of -specific- game knowledge could work against the system. 

I tried a few levels myself with the goal of trying to determine what information I was taking for granted based on being a human who has played somanygames over her life. 

My conclusion was that goals and planning are important, and the model/system is going to have to be able to figure out what the goal is over time with extremely limited information in an environment where exploration is heavily penalized (see: the scoring). Also important: being able to persist what's relevant so you don't have to start over each level within a game. 

For my initial approach, I'm combining models--vision for providing more context than just coordinates and colors, a text-based reasoning model for planning and decisioning, and a much smaller text-based model in charge of taking notes for the reasoning model to persist learnings for both a level and across levels.

Though you can't be 100% sure the game won't suddenly change the rules on you (see: control inversion, like left makes the character move right for a level), you can be -reasonably- sure that at least some of what you learn in a previous level will be transferrable to the next because that's how games work. Games build up a vocabulary of mechanics and iconography over time, and making sense of that (if you aren't a human) is non-trivial.  

Maybe this won't be what they're looking for, but the key challenge seems to me to be getting the correct type and amount of information to each model to make the best use of it without overwhelming any of them... and not being a blank slate between levels because that scoring penalty is -harsh-. 

Being spoiled for choice about what's important can leave models spinning in circles, so there probably also needs to be some sort of guidance mechanism to help knock it out of unproductive behavior cycles.

I hope this helps! 

[EDIT] I should also note that I've never been convinced that One Model To Rule Them All was ever going to be an effective way to get us to "AGI"... and my background is more software development/systems engineering than ML/data science. 

So to me, this is more a systems problem than a model-specific problem. 

Again, that may not be what they're looking for, but it was interesting enough for me to code in my actual free time, so I've learned things even if I don't end up submitting. :)

title: Provide some error info for competition submission?
author: zhengxuyu
text:
## Problem I encountered

When submitting a notebook to ARC-AGI-3, the only feedback we receive is the final score. I respect the rule, but the initial dry-run only outputs a dummy `submission.parquet`, which cannot fully represent what will happen when testing. We have zero visibility about whether the low score is caused by a poor agent or code bug or pipeline error. Is there any way to know whether some error pop out during testing at least?

## My Specific Issue

My agent is designed to run for approximately 6 hours (the full time budget). Locally, it runs for 5-8 hours without issues. However, on Kaggle, the competition rerun appears to complete in roughly **10 minutes**, which is far too short for 75 games. This suggests either:

1. The agent is crashing silently on startup (e.g., import error, weight loading failure, shape mismatch)
2. The agent is hitting an unhandled exception on each game and the Swarm skips to the next
3. There's a framework-level timeout or resource limit I'm not aware of
4. Some other environmental difference between the dry-run and the competition rerun

I have **no way to distinguish between these cases** without logs.

## What Would Help

Even minimal feedback would be transformative for debugging:

- **Error/no-error status**: Did the agent crash? Was there a Python exception?
- **stderr output**: Even just the last 100 lines of stderr from the rerun
- **Game count**: How many games did the agent actually played?
- **Runtime**: How long did the competition rerun actually take?
- **Basic metrics**: Total actions taken, games completed vs skipped

## Current Debugging Workflow (Painful)

1. Write agent code
2. Test locally — works fine
3. Submit to Kaggle — get a poor score
4. No idea why it's low — is the agent crashing? Running too slow? Playing badly?
5. Guess what might be wrong, change code, wait 24 hours (1 submission/day), repeat

This makes it extremely difficult to iterate on non-trivial agents. A simple error log would save days of blind debugging.

## What Others Have Said

I suspect other participants face the same issue. If your agent works locally but scores unexpectedly low on Kaggle, you're stuck guessing why.

## Suggestion

Could the competition provide at least one of:
- An error/success flag per game
- A summary of agent runtime and action counts? 

Thank you for considering this. The competition itself is fantastic — this small addition to the feedback loop would help everyone build better agents.

title: Some ideas on Approaches
author: aidetective
text:
In the past couple of months I have been creating a "general puzzle solver", where you enter the legal moves and win-conditions and it tries to solve it. Mainly with BFS, Mote-Carlo, state-hashing, and constraint-propagation methods. So this worked quite well for mazes, fox-chicken-corn-farmer puzzle, zebra-puzzle, tower-of-hanoi, sudoku, slitherlink, other pencil puzzles, 8-sliding puzzle,  8-queens, knights move, Tic-tac-toe, 4-coloring map, and a few more.

So the first thing I realised was that many simple "classic" AI problems don't need much reasoning and can be solved with tree-search, constraint propogation, and state-hashing and backtracking. Basically brute force. And this is not to be overlooked as it forms the backbone of any algorithm.

The second thing I realised was that it is easy to find counter examples for which this breaks. The simplest example is this:

A 100x100 white grid with 2 red squares and 2 green squares.

Legal move: when a red square is next to any other, turn that square red and the original red square white.

Win: No green squares left.

Just using tree-search and state-hashing is infeasible. The key to this is, I believe, is recognition of the problem. We have to recognise that this can be interpreted as 2 red agents and 2 goals. Then pick an algorithm (A* search with distance heuristic) to solve.

Other more general techniques are:

(1) Invariant finding: Noticing all moves fix the number of red squraes at 2 and green squares can only deplete. [This can be a bit tricky since some things are invariant for a certain time only]

(2) Splitting the problem: We notice we can pair up each red square with each green square and solve this as two concurrent puzzles. Also hard to recognise.

Some other observations:

People have studied this area in 

(1) General Game Playing (GGP)

(2) Planning Problems (PDDL/STRIPS)

One general thing from PDDL is the idea of ignoring delete lists to get a good admissible heuristic.

One of the hardest games to solve that is just at the edge of human solvability is Sokoban.

The general idea is just like there is not one general algorithm to solve any math problem, there will not be any one algorithm to solve any puzzle. So the idea is to use recognition and mix-and-match domain specific algorithms.

ARC-3 is a bit different in that you have to infer the rules. But once inferred you still have to have a good algorithm to solve it. So it's two hard problems in one!

title: Some ideas on Approaches
author: fchollet
text:
"Inferring the rules" is itself 3 distinct problems: exploring game space to collect data, turning the data into causal models of game mechanics, and inferring the goal(s). So in total you have 4 problems to solve:

- Exploration
- Modeling
- Goal setting
- Planning + execution (in the general case these are 2 different problems, but in ARC 3 they are basically merged into one)

The difficulty breakdown of each subproblem depends on the environment. But on average it should look something like:

- Exploration: 20% difficulty
- Modeling: 65% difficulty
- Goal setting: 10% difficulty (very game dependent, can be quite hard for some games and trivial for others)
- Planning + execution: 5% difficulty (mostly kicks in on latter levels; initial levels have ~0% difficulty on this axis)

title: Some ideas on Approaches
author: raviannaswamy
text:
I have been thinking along this lines too and wanted to add some observations.

I think at least six distinct stages are necessary for 'intelligent' solving of a game level.

1. Perceiver: reduction of pixel world into grid world (or list of entities and their spatial locations)
2. Scientist: learning of the properties and functions of each entity or each interaction of avatar with that entity.
3. Game Modeler: learning GOAL of the game, what gives final reward or intermediate reward, what punishes temporarily or terminally; figuring out PURPOSE of each entity or interaction in this path.
4. Milestone and Subroutine learner: ability to re-see the finished episodes not as a single chain of actions, but as sequence of state-changing milestones and the actions needed to go from each to the other.
5. Planner: Specifying in a new unsolved level through 'mental' simulation with current understanding, a solution in the form of sorties or subgoals or milestones.
6. Execution: Decomposing the sorties in an actual situation to arrive at action sequence - and using perception/scientist/modeling work again if there are new unknowns that thwart the plan.

To make this concrete, in the locksmith game. (SPOILER for those who have not played it)
1. Perceiver does not 'see' 64x64 image frame. They see playable area, HUD of battery life and lives, they see key map and lock and room.
2. Scientist (Exploration and Experimentation) finds out that touching a modifier changes the key shape or size or color. and that without that match touching lock is useless.
3. Game Modeler figures out that goal of the game is to transform key to match the target on door and approach the door (on level 1)
4. Milestone Subroutine learner learns where to go and what to do to change color, change shape or change orientation.
5. Planner first recognizes the sequence of milestones to solve the level. 
6. Execution simulates mentally what is needed for each milestone and milestone by milestone reaches the goal, recovering form mistakes.

The reason why humans excel in the games is we do not search in action space. We do not even search in state space. The planner searches in the sortie space or milestone space.
They done say move left move right in their solution. They say go to forge change shape, go to palette, paint, then rotate and go to door.
Planning happens at very sparse synthesis.

Each of the first 3 stages in a module in a data reduction cascade - it dramatically re-presents what data is worth paying attention to and transforms from spatial coordinates to invariant graph coordinates.

Perceiver transforms from pixel-space to grid space (condensing a 5x5 avatar or entity into a single point symbol)
Scientist connects which state-actions are of use and creates a state-action space with transition causal chains.
Game modeler and Milestone learner consolidate this information into a goal-back-driven tree that can help planner/executor derive programs.

Until the perceiver and scientist subset and re-present the pixel world into a state space, efficient game learning/planning/execution is impossible.

The reason chess and go play work so well is because they are already abstract grid worlds and further humans incorporate game model and milestone learning into search engines and planning becomes action-space search, which is actually a shame or cheating form of intelligence. brute force once decision tree is setup with heuristics to reduce burden a bit.

ARC-AGI-3 clearly exposes this gap and adding the action-budget is the brilliant stroke, because it forces us to realize that key to human efficiency is the ability to create transform spaces of perception and cognition WELL BEFORE game modeling begins. A possible 1000x data reduction from pixel worlds to object lists to rule-chains that are game-agnostic so that game goal discovery and semantic role labeling of entities can happen on this already small space. Game grammar induction.

Across game levels, we can then see which of the knowledge and skill and subroutines gained in a previous level carries over and what is new to be learned.

--

Modeling (in @fchollet note) I would split into world-modeling and game-modeling and bundle the goal discovery into that.
Planning and execution - I will split into two, one that outlines milestone reaching and remains stable guide for the execution-planner and executor.

--

To summarize, a good solution architecture REQUIRES where in symbolic fashion or neurosymbols:

- Perceiver: pixel grids to symbolic grid or entity lists
- Scientist: entity lists to rule lists
- Game Model: Goal, Milestone, Subroutines
- Planner: scene to milestone sequence and subgoal states
- Execution: Pathfinding from milestone to milestone with recovery from mistakes

This view also restates Comprehension as goal-directed compression of information. Compression itself is not as important as relevance filtering. Intelligence is the recognition of events that cause world-state to change for better or worse and noticing and remembering and consolidating the action/context/happening chains that lead each such state change. Intelligence is ability to chain them at will to reach a goal.

( I am planning to post this also as a separate discussion, which I plan to update frequently with my experiments and results)

Yes, but the relief I am seeing in my own instropective play is that each stage builds on previous stage and feeds back to it and refines it, but they are quite self contained otherwise.
In other words, once perceiver is fairly stable and customized for scientist, perceiver is frozen until next level new elements get introduced. Likewise once game comprehender understands the game goals and rules, scientist is pretty much done. Each stage that becomes an encoder-decoder that creates compact representation of what is necessary and complete to the next.

One big new think I am finding is that Planning happens in a graph (of entity relationships) that does not have spatial grid in mind. Execution happens in a grid world! In other words Planner says, rotate the key, change its color and shape and proceed to lock, executor translates it to real world and incorporates obstacle avoidance, etc. This is postponement of details that not only reduces cognitive load, it serves to create approximate solutions that can represent a manifold not a list of paths. This 'vagueness' of language is the virtue, aka abstraction.

author: aidetective
text:
Another point I might add, is that I still don't think a solution to ARC-3 would be yet AGI for this reason:

My belief is all the games will be able to be solved with combining known domain specific algorithms (maze search, jigsaw, symmetry matching...)

But, one could imagine a game that is equivalent to solving some hard unsolved math problem. (e.g. twin primes conjecture). And that cannot be solved just by algorithmically combining known piror algorithms but requires a "leap of thinking". Specifically, hard symbolic manipulation, analogy, generalisation and more. The key is the complexity of the world-model they can build. (And how self-refrenetial it is).

But we don't even have to go that far. I think even a moderately hard Sokoban puzzle might defeat the best AI's here. 

I could be wrong and that the AI's that solve ARC-3 are indeed so general that they could be applied to reasearch-type questions but I have my doubts at this stage. Thoughts?

title: Some ideas on Approaches
author: jacquelynnhall
text:
I am not entirely sure that the exact goal is to claim AGI. It seems to me more about: what kinds of problems do we have to solve to get there, and what might some of those solutions be?

While combinations of known solutions might get AI through individual levels, getting AI through the games with -a good score- is likely to require closer to what a human does. A human doesn't pattern match against every game they've ever played and decide on an algorithm. Well, this human doesn't. :) 

The test games look just enough like other games that treating the test games as if they -are- those games is its own specific form of trap, which the replays of the reasoning models that include their reasoning demonstrate. 

Personally, having played somanygames in my life, I see games as a form of language, so this is like "how quickly can you learn and apply this language?"

Actions are literally verbs. "Things on the board" are nouns. What happens when you apply verbs to the nouns teaches the grammar (game mechanics). 

Not all of the nouns are important, so which ones even matter, and is that situational? What is it about those pieces that makes you identify them as "mattering," and how can you impart that to a system that you can't coach after the run has started? 

Well-designed games, which these so far seem to be, don't expect you to know everything starting out. They give you a starting point and a list of actions and are like "GLHF" (good luck, have fun). 

When you first take an action, a person immediately knows more, even if they don't understand it. That leads to subconscious (sometimes conscious if the game's -really- hard) hypotheses that get tested, verified or negated, reformed. In the process, the mechanics reveal themselves over time. 

Not only that, but as you're absorbing the game's language, you can (frequently) apply it to later rounds. But doing so can either be easy (I see the same piece again, that's probably the thing I'm moving because last round involved moving a piece to another piece, and I see things that relate to the same goal state) or hard (okay, this level looks nothing like the first, what is it that I learned the last level that I could apply here). 

What I've been trying to do is to realize what I notice as I'm playing a level that I may be taking for granted. I identify things that look important. I do a thing to find out what happens. I update what's important based on that and the current board state, which may be radically different. 

I keep going until either I win, or I look at the game and go "nah" because I -know- what I'm supposed to do, and I don't want to because it's too fiddly. :D 

That's... not exactly how things work for AI. AI doesn't have memory, it needs that. It doesn't inherently have "I pressed left 3 times and some bar decreased in 3 times" because, unless you're just throwing everything at it, it doesn't inherently -know- it has done the same thing before (ever). 

To me, one of the issues is reliably getting clean enough information to determine what's important. Deterministic methods don't hold up well to the games' variety, and vision models I've tried haven't been precise enough. I'm currently trying to find a balance that can provide comprehension about what a distinct piece might be while also being precise enough that it can be used consistently in reasoning (within a level). 

What works for me--naming each piece 'this thingie' or 'that thingie'--isn't going to work for AI because it's not specific enough. I'm really associating the terms (even when I reuse them) with specific combinations of pixels that I've identified as meaningfully related, even though I haven't described them meaningfully (to anyone else). 

After that, it's about surfacing the relevant information at the right time--how to make the models pay attention to what's really important and/or impart some sense of what that is? 

And then, it's about generalizing. "I hit left, bar got smaller, I hit left, bar got smaller, I hit up, bar got smaller" is mechanical, state-based observation, not "when I hit one of the directional keys, the bar will get smaller." 

I mean, you can only have those kinds of observations in the first place if you know both "left is last thing that happened" and also "the bar is smaller now than it was last turn" at the same time. 

Holding the whole history of a level (much less a whole game) is going to be a lot to process. We don't work like that. Personally, I note the bar decreasing and go "okay, I'll pay attention to that if it seems to get low and I don't think I'm near the goal." 

But that kind of generalizing is one of the challenges. 

To top it all off, to get a -good- score, it isn't simply enough to win the level. If you aren't able to apply -something- to the next one, you'll be stuck wasting moves rediscovering things you should "already know." So we also have to solve how to store and surface that information. 

I could be wrong about all this, by the way. :) It's just my understanding, and why I find the problem space so fascinating. 

I also want to compliment the games' designer(s). They're benevolently evil in a specific sort of way, and I'm here for it.

BTW. Interpreting the puzzle from the rules seems to be something an LLM is really good at. (Sometimes!) 
For example I asked chatGPT:
```python
Intrpret this puzzle: 
A 100x100 white grid with 2 red squares and 2 green squares. 
Legal move: when a red square is next to any other, turn that square red and the original red square white. 
Win: No green squares left.
```
Answer from ChatGPT:
```python
[...]
🧠 Key insight

Red squares behave like mobile agents that can:

Move around the board
“Overwrite” other colors (including green)

So effectively:

A red square can walk onto a green square and erase it
❗ Important constraint

You only ever have 2 red squares at a time (since moving one removes it from its original spot).

🎯 What’s the goal?

Remove all green squares (i.e., turn them red at some point).

💡 Can you always win?

Yes — and here’s why:

Each red square can move freely across the grid (like a sliding piece).
There are only 2 green squares.
You have 2 independent red movers.

So:

Send each red square toward a green square.
When a red steps onto a green, that green is eliminated.
Repeat until both greens are gone.
...

```

Which is exactly right! Trying to write code that could recognise this from the rules is much harder (but perhaps still worth doing). 
So at least in this simple case, LLMs seem to be a good recognition tool.

edit: Although it did miss something out: If the two green "goals" are close to one of the red "movers". Then that mover should collect both goals, that would be most optimum.

title: Stop searching the Action Tree, Discover the Transformation Graph (milestone chain)
author: raviannaswamy
text:
Solving arc-agi-3 needs a truly principled mechanism that takes best ideas from curiosity driven learning (schmidhuber), world modeling work (Ha, Dreamer), hierarchical RL, affordance learning, robotics and add something many of them may not have - symbolic substrate and semantic overlay of actors, actions, events. I am formulating something to this effect using Panini's karaka theory as the framework for understanding and registering actions/affordances.

Even though the games from @fchollet look like happening in a physical visual world, they are actually symbolic grid worlds rendered as visual worlds. Only one or two of them are truly non-styled physical world such as valve check, robot legs and squigee painter (crane?). Unfortunately the rendering is what blocks LLMs to peer into them. But the good news is, once that obstacle is overcome by developing either a hand coded or learned adapter than translates the frame sequence into a scene graph, the next layer innovation of above-said exploration-driven, but game-goal-driven learning can happen.

This arcprize benchmark @gregkamradt is definitely one benchmark that demands a rethink beyond supervised learning (data to label), semi-supervised learning (data to data-as-label), reinforcement learning (environment to action-sequence) to a new framework which I want to call: Interactive Cartography or more precisely, Narrative-role Cartography. Like Curiosity learning, it is goal-free exploration, but directed by need to make a narrative. It captures results not in scalars, as robotics does, but in an scene graph or dynamic scene graph.

You explore a world to catalog what is where and what happens when this touches that etc. And what precondition or transformation is needed to what to make it useful for what.

Then you turn this world model into purposive planning - what set of conditions need to solved in what sequence to meet a goal condition.

author: aidetective
text:
Very interesting thoughts.
I think tree-search is a non-starter anyway, since don't you only have a limited set of moves?
Unless you can run the puzzles "off-line" which we are still not clear about if that is legal or not(!)

What might be the list of meaningful assignments one might make?

* "An agent" - a set of pixels that translates in different directions when you press arrow keys
* "A mover" - a set of pixels the may move each go independent of your actions (Could be friend or foe)
* "A wall" - pixels that stop your agent moving.
* "A door" - a wall but of different color that perhaps may be changeable
* "A box" - something that can be pushed
* "A destroyable" - something that can be destroyed perhaps by clicking
* "A goal" - something your agent needs to move towards
* "A hurdle" - something an agent can jump over
* "A matchable" - part of an object which you can match with part of another object
* "An avatar" - some symbol which matches with another thing in the game
* "A collectable" - a sub-goal
* "Energy bar" - your energy if it runs out you lose
* "Score bar" - you want to increase this
* "Life indicators"
* "A transporter" - agents can transport through these to other places
* "A raft" - agents can sit on these 
* "A button" - changes something in the game
* "A placeable" - something which can be dragged in place
* "An escalator" - moving walkway or river
* (Please suggest more!)

To be honest I don't think any human will be able to code all these things. It will have to be an LLM that can interpret this. 😭

These are the ones suggested by GPT:

```python
🧠 State & Conditions
A key – unlocks a specific door or trigger
A lock – requires a matching key or condition
A switch (toggle) – flips between states (on/off)
A pressure plate – activates only while something is on it
A timer – triggers events after some steps
A countdown object – disappears or changes after N turns
A checkpoint – saves progress / respawn point
A stateful tile – changes appearance/behavior after interaction
⚙️ Movement & Physics Variants
A slippery tile – agent keeps moving until hitting something
A conveyor splitter – redirects movement in multiple directions
A teleporter pair network – multiple linked transporters
A gravity field – pulls objects in a direction each tick
A rotating platform – changes orientation over time
A one-way tile – allows movement only in one direction
A moving platform – carries the agent along a path
🧱 Interaction Objects
A container – can hold other objects (like boxes or keys)
A crafting station – combines items into new ones
A duplicator – creates copies of objects
A modifier tile – changes properties (color, size, speed)
A fuse – connects triggers to effects (like logic wiring)
A trigger zone – activates when agent enters an area
🧩 Puzzle Mechanics
A color mixer – combines colors to create new rules
A pattern lock – requires arranging elements in a shape
A mirror/reflector – redirects beams or movement
A beam emitter – shoots lines that interact with objects
A logic gate – AND/OR conditions for activation
A sequence trigger – must activate things in order
👾 Agents & Behaviors
A chaser – follows the player
A patroller – moves in a fixed path
A random walker – stochastic movement
A guard with vision cone – reacts if it “sees” the agent
A follower – trails behind the player
A neutral NPC – interacts but isn’t hostile
A spawner – creates new movers or enemies
💥 Hazards & Combat
A hazard tile – damages or kills on contact
A projectile – moves independently and causes effects
A trap – activates under certain conditions
A shield – temporarily blocks damage
An area-of-effect zone – affects multiple tiles at once
📦 Inventory & Resources
An inventory system – agent carries items
A consumable – one-time-use item
A resource node – can be harvested repeatedly
A currency – used for unlocking or scoring
An upgrade – permanently improves abilities
🧭 Meta / Rule-Based Elements (very ARC-like)
A rule tile – changes the game rules dynamically
A transformation rule – e.g., “all red becomes blue”
A cloning rule – objects replicate under conditions
A constraint tile – limits actions (e.g., no turning)
A goal modifier – changes what counts as winning
🌍 Environment & Meta Structure
A fog-of-war tile – hides unseen areas
A boundary/edge rule – wrap-around or solid edges
A level portal – moves to another level/state
A script trigger – executes predefined logic
A randomness seed tile – introduces controlled randomness
```

I see. And do you know the formula is?Edit: On further reading the score for each level is:

 $$\text{score}_{level} = Min\left(1.15, \left(\frac{\text{human turns}}{\text{AI turns}}\right)^2\right)$$

Then the game score (e.g. for 4 levels) is given by:

Per-game score = Weighted average of level scores (weighted by level index, 1-indexed).
Total score = Average of all individual game scores.

text: How I'm interpreting it, is that there is a human baseline score. Every time you move, or make an action, except scanning the board, which a human would do through vision. So if you try to brute force the answer, your percentage drops unless you solve in fewer turns than a human. That took me a while to figure out. author: raviannaswamy
text:
I have been thinking about what is it that a successful agent need to learn from each game it encounters.
As an example, I put together this in two parts - a game spec (only for context) and the actual set of rules that try define the ls20 game (Locksmith) concisely. You can think of this as the core engine described as rules in following categories: Places, Entities, Actions, Interactions, Events, Goal Requirements, Obstacles...

How to represent this ruleset as rule-data that can be acquired, updated and used for planning and execution is important and is key to building a continual learning agent, but I felt this de-finition might be helpful first step since it bounds what needs to be gathered about a game before designing further. We can take each game-rule or fact and ask: What perception/probing/planning/observing mechanism is needed to learn this? Even that question shows where symbolic systems and neural systems may struggle and how we may need to fix each or make hybrid or invent something fundamentally atomic and groundbreaking that treats all layers just data at various levels of granularity!

I have taken help from Claude Opus and Gemini for editing and improving my draft.

Comments welcome.

# 1. LS20 "Locksmith" — Game Design Spec

## Core Concept

Locksmith is a **grid-based key-matching puzzle** played on a 64x64 pixel grid (effective 13x12 navigable cells). The player controls a character that carries an invisible "key" defined by three properties: **shape** (6 options), **color** (4 options), and **rotation** (4 options: 0/90/180/270 degrees). The goal in each level is to step onto one or more **locks**, but a lock only opens when the player's key configuration exactly matches its requirements. If it doesn't match, the lock acts like a wall and blocks entry.

The player transforms their key by stepping on **modifier tiles** scattered across the map — each one cycles a single key property to its next value. The twist: modifiers only cycle forward (shape +1 mod 6, color +1 mod 4, rotation +90), so reaching a target state may require multiple passes through the same modifier.

A **step budget** (42 per attempt) creates time pressure. **Batteries** refill the counter. **Pushers** (directional pistons) teleport the player across the map. Some modifiers are **NPC wanderers** that patrol autonomously — the player must intercept them at the right moment. Three lives; running out of steps costs one life and resets the level.

## The Design Arc: Progressive Complexity

The 7 levels follow a textbook curriculum design, introducing exactly one new concept per level, then combining them:

---

### Level 1 — "The Tutorial"
- **New concepts:** Movement, step counter, walls, rotation modifier, lock matching
- **Task:** Key needs 1 rotation change. One static rotation modifier. One lock.
- **Skill learned:** The fundamental loop — *examine the lock's requirement, find a modifier, transform the key, return to the lock*. The player also discovers that locks block you when the key doesn't match (this looks like a wall but isn't).

### Level 2 — "The Moving Target"
- **New concepts:** NPC wanderers, batteries, death/reset
- **Task:** Key needs 3 rotation changes. The rotation modifier is a moving NPC. Two batteries.
- **Skill learned:** Modifiers can move — you must **intercept** them by bouncing on/off their patrol cell. Batteries are essential for long routes. Route ordering matters (which battery to collect when). Death teaches that running out of steps resets everything.

### Level 3 — "Two Modifier Types"
- **New concepts:** Color modifier, pushers
- **Task:** Key needs 1 color change + 2 rotation changes. Both modifier types present. Pushers create shortcuts.
- **Skill learned:** **Multi-modifier sequencing** — the Strategist must decide the order: color first, then rotations, with a battery in between. Pushers act as teleport edges in the navigation graph, saving many steps.

### Level 4 — "Shape Enters"
- **New concepts:** Shape modifier
- **Task:** Key needs 3 color changes + 1 shape change. Heavy pusher network.
- **Skill learned:** The third key property (shape) works identically to color/rotation — just another cyclic modifier. The pusher network dominates navigation. One exploratory death to map the level, then a clean solve.


### Level 5 — "Mastery Test"
- **New concepts:** None
- **Task:** 3 color changes + 4 rotation changes, 3 batteries, 2 rotation modifier locations, long route.
- **Skill learned:** Pure **strategic execution**. The most complex route so far (7 sub-goals, 3 battery interleaves), but no new mechanics. Tests whether the player has internalized the pattern.

### Level 6 — "Multi-Lock"
- **New concepts:** Two locks with different requirements, 3+ NPCs creating noise
- **Task:** Open Lock A (red key) then Lock B (blue key). Multiple NPC modifiers patrol the map, causing accidental key changes.
- **Skill learned:** **Lock ordering** (open whichever lock is closest in key-state-space first), and **reactive planning** (NPCs change your key unpredictably, so you must monitor and adapt rather than follow a fixed plan). This is the strategic capstone.

### Level 7 — "Fog of War"
- **New concepts:** Limited visibility (~4-cell radius)
- **Task:** Same as Level 5 mechanically (3 color changes + rotation), but under fog. The player cannot see the map.
- **Skill learned:** **Exploration under uncertainty**. Attempt 1 is sacrificial — purely mapping batteries, pushers, and modifier locations. Attempt 2 uses that mental map to execute efficiently. 

# LS20 Rules - distilled from game understanding (what the agent must learn live)

## Places
* The game takes place on a two-dimensional grid measuring 64x64 tiles.
* Some environments feature a "Fog" condition that dynamically obscures all map elements located further than a 20.0 unit distance from the player.

## Entities
* **Player**: A user-controlled character sprite that moves across the grid and carries a "key" state.
* **Key**: The current state of the player, defined simultaneously by three properties: shape, color, and rotation.
* **Locks**: Stationary sprites that restrict access based on key requirements.
* **Goal Indicators**: Visual elements that display the exact shape, color, and rotation properties required to bypass specific locks.
* **Modifiers**: Tile sprites that alter a specific property of the player's key.
* **Batteries**: Consumable item sprites that interact with the step counter.
* **Pushers**: Directional entities programmed to forcefully move other sprites.
* **NPCs**: Autonomous entities that follow calculated patrol paths and can carry modifier properties.
* **Walls**: Static, collidable blocks that restrict movement.

## Events
* **Level Completion**: Triggered when the player successfully steps on all lock entities in the current map.
* **Level Reset**: Triggered when the step counter reaches zero, which resets the player's position, reverts their key state, and consumes one life.
* **Game Over**: Triggered when the player's available lives drop to zero.

## Actions
* The player can move one tile per turn in four cardinal directions: up, down, left, or right.

## Interactions
* **Shape Modification**: Stepping on a shape modifier cycles the player's current key shape to the next sequential shape in the game's registry.
* **Color Modification**: Stepping on a color modifier cycles the player's key color to the next index.
* **Rotation Modification**: Stepping on a rotation modifier rotates the player's key forward by 90 degrees.
* **Battery Consumption**: Moving onto a battery sprite consumes it and immediately refills the player's step counter back to its maximum capacity.
* **Lock Rejection**: Attempting to step on a lock when the player's key properties do not perfectly match results in the player's movement being blocked, treating the lock as a solid wall.
* **Pusher Collision**: If a pusher entity collides with the player, it forces the player to move continuously in the pusher's specific direction until the player hits an obstacle.
* **NPC Patrols**: Every time the player executes a movement action, patrolling NPCs advance one step along their designated paths.

## Goal Requirements
* To successfully open any lock, the player must configure their key's shape, color, and rotation to perfectly match the target properties encoded into that lock.
* To advance to the next level, the player must resolve and eliminate every single lock present on the current grid.

## Obstacles
* A strict step counter decreases incrementally with every player action, functioning as a movement budget.
* The player is restricted to a maximum of three lives (attempts) per level.
* Wall sprites physically obstruct navigation, forcing the player to calculate longer routes.
* Locks act as physical barriers blocking pathways until the correct key combination is formed.
* Fog conceals the level layout, requiring the player to memorize routes and explore blindly.

title: Introducing ARC3.Games: Browser-Based ARCEngine Game Player & Gameplay Database
author: gijsschenk
text:
In short, ARC3.Games is an open source, browser-based ARCEngine game player connected to an open database that stores gameplay.

Why? Initially as part of porting [PushWorld](https://deepmind-pushworld.github.io/play/) to the ARCEngine, to have a more user-friendly way to interact with games. There is the game player on the ARCPrize website, but it is baked into the site, and not open source, so you can't play your custom games with it. The [ARC-AGI Tookit](https://docs.arcprize.org/toolkit/overview) is just for letting computers play the games, with primitive rendering capabilities, and nothing much for humans.

Another reason for ARC3.Games is to crowdsource gameplay data to be used for creating capable AI agents. Each time a player finishes a level, their performed action sequence gets sent to the server, verified, and put into the open database, accessible through the API. Only action sequences that finish a level get recorded; game overs do not. Resets do not get recorded either. When a player resets a game, the action sequence for that level gets cleared.

Unlike the ARCPrize game player, ARC3.Games loads the games locally instead of playing them on a remote server through an API. This is done through a virtual Python environment in the browser, enabled by [PyScript](https://pyscript.net/).

There are 30 games in the library: 25 public games, 4 public preview games, and the PushWorld port ("pw14-c1586e55"), which is a partial port — just the games that would fit within the 64x64 frame.

Check it out:
https://arc3.games/

title: Generating training data ideas?
author: aidetective
text:
If we are to use the standard neural network approach to this task, then we would need to generate lots of training data.

One method might be to get lots of old computer games (e.g. Atari) and put it in the right format for training.

Another method which I want to talk about is generating novel games. This seems extremely hard to do! To generate genuinely interesting games automatically, would not only give you valuable training data for this puzzle, but you could essentially repackage it as a mobile app as "Infinite fun games" to play. And make a gazillion dollars.

So this gives at least 2 motivations for creating software to generate interesting puzzles. 

First question:

* Would an app capable of generating interesting games also necessarily be advanced enought to solved them? Or can we separate the two?

Let's assume that we can create the puzzles, perhaps by starting from a solution and jumbling it backwards. This would not always create a puzzle that is humanly possible to solve. (e.g. imagine jumbling up a rubix cube - it is notoriously easier to jumble than it is to solve). 

Then we have the question of how to assemble both a set of rules/game mechanics and suitable starting and end states. One might try to compose different things like mazes, key/door, transporter, gravity, snakes, buttons, etc. But not all compositions would make for interesting games. Or one could imagine a more emergent system where simple rules might generate emergent mechanics without having them specified. (A maze might grow like a tree from a seed). 

Another problem is that our generated puzzles may not intersect with the type of puzzles in this competition.

I think only a machine trained on hours of youtube videos of puzzles and games will have any hope of solving the puzzles at human-level. And such a neural network will not fit into the memory allowed.

Packaging the puzzles into nxn coloured grids gives us the false impression that mechanical calculation is enough to solve the puzzles whereas indeed we need the sum-of-total-human-knowledge in order to solve them.

What's your thoughts on this matter?

title: Generating training data ideas?
author: mattpoetker
text:
My take is that a ground-up RL or ML model by itself isn't going to be enough for ARC-AGI 3 because these games require prior knowledge about things like gravity/physics, cause-and-effect, and familiar representations like 'buttons', 'switches', etc. Plus, it requires the skill of planning ahead, and adapting as dynamics/rules change or compound. An RL model doesn't just learn this high-level thought process without an entirely different method of training and model architecture. I don't think generating more games to train on unlocks this higher level thought process.

World models (like [Dreamer v4](https://danijar.com/project/dreamer4/)) have shown promising planning ability, but they're planning over **known dynamics and environments** with clear reward signals. With ARC, figuring out the dynamics and rules **is** the task. You have to discover through exploration and then form an 'understanding' of the game in some persistent way.

Vision-enabled LLM's have already shown great results in solving levels of ARC-AGI 3, but the T4 VRAM constraints of the kaggle competition limit the 'intelligence' of the open source models that can be used.

text:

One thing I'm not yet sure about is whether the algorithm will need inbuilt algorithms like A* search or such like or whether it will learn these algorithms on it's own. Indeed it is quite hard to say if humans have in built search algorithms or if it is just emergent from simpler rules.

I did once envisage that the brain may be able to "reset" itself to a previous state and re-run simulations with certain pathways disabled. But that might just be fanciful and it maybe be doing it more in a software rather than hardware manner.

title: Generating training data ideas?
author: opfromthestart
text:
I think an approach of generating lots of training examples would be necessary to complete this. The leading result in ARC-AGI-2, NVARC, won as a result of having a hundred thousand training examples that were generated mostly synthetically from mashups of public puzzles. I think porting existing puzzle games (someone has already done The Witness, i am looking at hard and varied sokobanlikes like Baba is You or Squishcraft) is probably the first necessary step.

From the NVARC approach, a large number(~2k) of non-synthetic examples are needed. This could be gotten from existing games, or from a game jam targeted at novel games compatible with the ARC-AGI-3 game engine. This would probably be better further into the competition as how well the current leaderboard does on your game would be a big indicator(negatively correlated of course) of how useful the game is.

Many puzzle games(take sudoku for example) can be generated in P time but take NP time to solve, so I do not believe that just being able to generate an arbitrary number of good-quality games would be enough to have a system perform well on another game, especially so since ARC has said that the private/test set games are out-of-distribution with respect to the public games.

I should clarify my statement from my first response. Saying "I don't think generating more games to train on..." I was referring to the limitations of DRL models that are trained from the ground-up. LLM SFT + RL on synthetic games could very well unlock much higher and efficient levels of performance and improve generalization.

title: Generating training data ideas?
author: russellutke
text:
My thinking is that an AGI model would have the capacity to operate at the level of domain-agnostic information, so like raw strings of real or binary values. At the highest level of abstraction, detecting patterns in any substrate is equivalent to finding a compressed representation of the information in that substrate (see algorithmic information theory). One might then be tempted to create training data by finding all compressions for strings up to some arbitrary length, and then training a transformer on those strings so it learns "general pattern recognition". The problem with this is that "finding all compressions" is actually incomputable, so you'd have to approximate it by working from specific models like CFGs, Markov models, combinations of sinusoidal functions, etc. 

But that might work? Just generate tons of synthetic "patterned" strings in this universal language of information by randomly generating various kinds of string generators and whatnot and use that to train a transformer. Then for a task like the ARC-3 it might be able to tease out order from chaos by compressing the stream of raw temporal data. Probably not efficient enough tbh, like others have said this challenge likely assumes too much prior knowledge - it's easy for humans because we have implicit knowledge of the various mechanisms already, it's not all sussed out from scratch during the game.

Better containers
author: michaelpoluektov
text:
TLDR: please allow us to pick our own Docker image for a submission

Why:

A good solution for this competition will likely involve the following:
- An LLM inference framework (VLLM, SGLang, TGI etc.)
- Many isolated sandboxes for untrusted code execution
- Potentially test-time training/fine-tuning of models

Managing and installing all of these things from a Jupyter notebook is very annoying. You effectively need to reverse engineer the Kaggle environment. It's quite unlikely that most of the pre-installed dependencies in the container will be used by many competitors (Who needs TensorFlow?)

On top of the engineering for the competitors, forcing people to find a way to install all of their dependencies from this environment will likely cost a lot in compute time: if it takes 5 minutes just to unpack and install a VLLM wheel, and competitors will use H100s, then each minimal test run will use an extra 5 minutes of H100 time. 

If an hour of H100 time costs 2$, and the average team saves a kernel 5 times a day over 4 months, it will cost you an extra 100$ per team in compute time, just run unpack and install VLLM dependencies for each saved notebook version.

The solution is simple: just allow us to submit a Docker image instead of a notebook. Or a Docker image that serves a jupyter notebook, whichever one is easier. That way, we can create the image once, install all the heavy requirements, and just load it without having to reverse engineer anything.

title: Better containers
author: mattpoetker
text: Aside from basic library installs (via pip install, etc.) any compiled binaries (llama.cpp for example), models/weights, large datasets, can be uploaded as a 'Dataset' on Kaggle and then referenced in your notebook so you only have to set it up once. If you're doing fine-tuning, you can do it in a one-off notebook then upload to Kaggle afterwards to get the most out of your submission time allotment.

title: Better containers
author: infinitecreativity
text:
I think this is one hand a good idea, on another, not really possible.

The way the scoring is setup, there is a gateway that captures HTTP requests on the Arcade actions to create the scorecard. They effectively run this gateway to see what you are doing. If you submit a container you would have to do finicky things with the network traffic.

On the other hand I agree, I am trying to reverse-engineer the container too, so it would be nice to know more / have more freedom.

title: [Resource] ARC-AGI-3 Logic & Action Metadata
author: karnakbaevarthur
text:
I’ve mapped the rules and controls for the first levels of ARC-AGI-3 tasks to help everyone get their agents up and running faster. I'm actively extending this, but here is the initial breakdown.

[**Dataset**](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/karnakbaevarthur/arc-agi-3-all-tasks-explanation)

This is a work in progress and I’ll be adding more tasks regularly. Feedback and contributions are welcome. If you notice anything missing or have suggestions for improvements, drop a comment. I’m keeping this updated as we go!

**What's inside:**
* **Game Logic:** Short descriptions of the goal, primary mechanics, and game description.
* **Action Mapping:** A simple reference for what the 4 directional keys, "tap" and "special move" do in each environment.
* **Level-by-Level:** A quick guide on how rules and constraints evolve from Level 1 to 10.

**How to use this:**
* **LLM Grounding:** Feed these text explanations to your LLM so it "understands" the rules before acting on the grid.
* **Pattern Matching:** Use the metadata to group similar problems (e.g., tasks that share gravity or mirroring logic).
* **Task Routing:** Help your agent select the right solver based on the task description.

[Dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/karnakbaevarthur/arc-agi-3-all-tasks-explanation)

Good luck :)
