title: Score discrepancy on submissions despite high local sim — request scoring trace (Human LB #1)
author: ryanxatlasai
text:
Hi Kaggle staff and ARC team,

  I'm the current Human Leaderboard #1 on ARC-AGI-3
  (FuFront-AI-RyanX-Atlas-AGI, 100.00 / 25 games / 183 levels / 6176 actions),
  verified on arcprize.org/leaderboard.

  My agent reproduces 0.96+ in local simulation using the official
  arc_agi-0.9.8 SDK. Across 6 Kaggle submissions since 2026-04-30,
  my publicScore has been:

  ┌────────────┬─────────────┐
  │    Date    │ publicScore │
  ├────────────┼─────────────┤
  │ 2026-04-30 │ 0.19        │
  ├────────────┼─────────────┤
  │ 2026-05-01 │ 0.00        │
  ├────────────┼─────────────┤
  │ 2026-05-02 │ 0.00        │
  ├────────────┼─────────────┤
  │ 2026-05-03 │ 0.00        │
  ├────────────┼─────────────┤
  │ 2026-05-04 │ 0.00        │
  ├────────────┼─────────────┤
  │ 2026-05-05 │ 0.04        │
  └────────────┴─────────────┘

  Mentioning the leaderboard standing only as a priority signal — I'm
  flagging this because the gap between local-sim and Kaggle-public score
  is large enough that I think it warrants a scoring-infra look rather
  than another agent iteration on my side.

  Capability context (not the main ask)

  This is not a toy replay script. My agent has also solved a separate
  RX185-style challenge that tests source-aware reasoning, phase tracking,
  memory snapshots, and deterministic strategy construction beyond
  ordinary leaderboard trace replay.

  I am not attaching private solver code, traces, or internal tooling
  publicly. If the ARC team wants to verify this capability, I can share
  a redacted RX185 challenge packet or arrange a private reproduction
  channel.

  The reason I mention RX185 is to clarify that the current Kaggle issue
  is unlikely to be explained by "the agent simply cannot solve ARC-style
  environments." The problem I am asking you to inspect is the
  scoring/runtime path: dataset mount, agent invocation, game IDs,
  gateway interaction, timeout, and stderr.

  What I'd like to request

  1. A scoring trace for one of my failed submissions
  (e.g., 2026-05-05, publicScore 0.04): which stage failed
  (parquet load / agent import / SDK call / timeout / CUDA cap),
  with stderr if available.
  2. Confirmation of which artifact is actually scored:
  submission.parquet or my_agent.py?
  3. Documented guidance on locking T4×2 accelerator on
  kaggle kernels push — pushes appear to default to P100, which
  silently breaks INT4/AWQ/FP8 model kernels (sm_75+ required).
  Currently the only workaround I know is the UI flip
  (Settings → Session options → Accelerator → GPU T4×2 → Save & Run All).

  Three observations that suggest scoring-infra rather than agent quality

  These are observations, not proven claims — happy to be corrected:

  - (a) Possible parquet pass-through. Across multiple of my submissions
  with different leaderboard scores, the resulting submission.parquet
  appeared identical in size (2648 bytes). This suggests the scoring
  path may invoke my_agent.py against server-side game instances rather
  than reading the parquet. Could you confirm?
  - (b) P100 vs T4×2 reset on push. As above; reproducible by anyone
  using AWQ/INT4 models.
  - (c) Possible env-hash drift on ka59. In a 24-trace replay audit
  on a server-style runtime, 23/24 PASSed but ka59 FAILed despite
  WIN on the public local SDK. If server-side game instances re-init
  with a different RNG seed than the public SDK exposes, agents that
  infer per-game state could break silently. Can you confirm
  hash-identity policy?

  Account / identifier (public-safe)

  - Kaggle user: ryanxatlasai
  - Competition: arc-prize-2026-arc-agi-3
  - Kernels involved (11 versions): ryanx-agi, ryanx-agi-0501,
  ryanx-agi-0504, r0503-graph-inline-fix, plus
  notebook{ce398f99b8, 2c5a3843d2, 26721c089f, b76fa0bb8c,  06460cfeea, b64ebd4c60, c130988125}.

  I'd prefer to forward my_agent.py, the trace .jsonl, and any
  detailed log via a private secure channel (Kaggle DM, ARC team
  private email, or any escalation route you prefer) rather than attach
  publicly. Please reply with a preferred channel.

  Thanks.

  ---

author: thezetaproject
text:
I don't like that the leaderboard is below 1%.

Here's an approach that might help those who are fine tuning models or using CPU/algorithm approaches:

[https://github.com/libretro-thumbnails/libretro-thumbnails](https://github.com/libretro-thumbnails/libretro-thumbnails)

This is the Retro Arch Thumbnail Repository.
It has over 54 Thousands Screenshots of In-Game Play for Consoles from Commodore 64,atari, nes and more all the classics.

One could argue that this amounts to nearly a large percentage of all the games ever commonly played.

Using this dataset, you can train a model, or use an llm to parse and classify these.

I believe this dataset alone if properly used should be enough to inform the game priors needed combined with the multimodal llms understanding of the game to classify the type of solutions needed to beat that type of game from just the screenshot alone.

Over the past few weeks, I've done something like this:
retro_snaps_catalog_classified.md 

Its not perfect, but its a decent categorization.

I also decided to map all the offline/public games against the distribution to see where the games fell, and how the games clustered to different solution types. 

I was then able to use that information and also chart the types of developmental skills needed to beat those games (i.e: by proxy you can estimate the efficacy of your agents).

 If you think of negative or subtractive clustering, you could probably guess the categories of games not being delivered in the public set, and give your agents more experience training against them.

If you have the means to actually train your agents to play the games with something like bizhawk emulator, (that's a good method).

My method of just relying on the screenshot was just for speed.

I hope this helps people pair their architectures with some better labeled data than just training from the public set.

Diffusion of memory?
author: thezetaproject
text:
Any random or brute force algorithm could “solve” arc 3 agi over time with stored memory of sequences. Those level sequences would then be chained together to give the appearance of intelligent learning.

That explains away a good portion of non-kaggle based “solutions”.

Llms are stuck due to their active storage limited to context window size, and the constraints of the competition not allowing models to write offline


Concept:

Why don't we use diffusion on memory/ storage of the correct game sequences?

Using the public set as training data you can use any method you like (cheap DFS/BFS) to derive the correct sequences then use the diffusion technique on those sequences and sequences chains (i.e to get the manifold).

The same way we took perfect images to train on and added random noise to destroy the image and reverse it, lets do the same with memories or sequence storage/solvers so that via diffusion the system will be able to generate a coherent sequence with the given level data?

**Don't train on the hard problem. 
Train on verified solutions to easy instances of the problem.**

title: How is the 1.30 on the LB possible?
author: yieldsmarter
text:
As the methodology states:
The maximum score per level is capped at 1.15x human baseline. If an AI discovers a shortcut and completes a level faster than humans, it can receive at most 1.15.
Doesn't this mean the best case would be beating each human baseline resulting in 1.15?

title: How is the 1.30 on the LB possible?
author: gregkamradt
text:
> Doesn't this mean the best case would be beating each human baseline resulting in 1.15?

Yes, per level you can score up to 1.15x. This gets capped at 100% per game. You can't score >100% on a game

We talk more about it in our scoring section here
https://arcprize.org/blog/arc-agi-3-human-dataset

title: Correcting an Error in Competition Submission Limits
author: macruzbar
text:
Hi everyone,

We want to sincerely apologize for a recent oversight regarding the daily submission limits for this competition, and share how we are addressing it.

#### What happened:
Our intended setting for this competition had been one submission per day. However, on May 27, a miscommunication over a mismatch between our settings and the written rules caused us to mistakenly change the competition settings to allow 5 submissions per day.

#### The Impact:
During this 13-day window, the system allowed up to 5 submissions per day. Understandably, several teams utilized these available submissions to test and improve their models. We want to be entirely clear that we do not view this as cheating or breaking the rules; teams were simply operating within the limits our system presented to them.

#### Going forward:
To get back to the intended course, we are taking the following steps:
- **Restoring the Cap:** Yesterday, June 8, we restored the submission limit back to one submission per day.
- **Invalidating Surplus Submissions:** We are working now to invalidate any additional submissions teams made after their first successful submission for each day during that period. title: Correcting an Error in Competition Submission Limits
author: ruichardliu
text:
Hi María and the Kaggle team, thanks for the transparency. But I'd like to point out a problem with this fix.

Invalidating the surplus submissions doesn't actually remove the advantage they created. During those 13 days, teams who submitted up to 5 times per day ran 50-60 extra experiments and learned exactly which approach scored best and what their ceiling was. That knowledge can't be erased. After the cap was restored, they can simply re-submit their already-validated best solution once, and the score comes right back. So deleting the records does not reset anyone to an equal footing - the real edge was the feedback/information from all those trials, not the submission count itself.

Meanwhile, the teams actually penalized by this rollback are the ones who played it safe or submitted less - they lose positions through no fault of their own, while the teams who exploited the extra attempts keep the insight.

A fairer option: rather than deleting valid submissions that everyone equally had the right to make, grant the same extra-submission budget to teams who joined the competition before the bug appeared but didn't get to benefit from it. That way everyone gets comparable opportunity to explore, instead of only some teams keeping the knowledge while others are pushed down the leaderboard. At minimum, please acknowledge this was a platform bug and avoid arbitrarily voiding submissions that were made entirely within the limits the system presented.

Thanks for considering this.

title: [Dataset] ARC-AGI-3 Human Trajectory Dataset on Hugging Face – Fueling Top-Down Action Planning?
author: magicsword001
text:
I believe that relying solely on "bottom-up" approaches like reinforcement learning has inherent limitations when it comes to training AI for long-term action planning. However, if we have access to "expert" action planning data—similar to gameplay logs of players clearing a game—we should be able to train models on action planning using a "top-down" approach. Recently, the human gameplay data from the ARC-AGI-3 environment was released here: [ARC-AGI-3 Human Dataset](https://arcprize.org/blog/arc-agi-3-human-dataset) To make this data more accessible for implementation, I’ve registered the dataset on Hugging Face. If we can leverage imitation learning to mimic how humans solve these tasks, I'm confident it will give AI a massive boost in long-term action planning.
The repository is here: 👉[magic-sword/arc_agi_3_public_demo_human_testing](https://huggingface.co/datasets/magic-sword/arc_agi_3_public_demo_human_testing) I have also published a Kaggle Notebook that demonstrates both **how I uploaded this data to Hugging Face** and **how to load and use it** in your own workflows. You can check it out here: 👉 [ARC-AGI-3 Public Demo Human Testing (Hugging Face)](https://www.kaggle.com/code/magicsword001/arc-agi-3-public-demo-human-testing-hugging-face?scriptVersionId=325811099) Here is a quick overview of how you can use it: ### 1. Analyzing with Pandas DataFrame ```python import pandas as pd from datasets import load_dataset repo_id = "magic-sword/arc_agi_3_public_demo_human_testing" dataset = load_dataset(repo_id, split="train") # Exclude the heavy 'trajectory' column to save memory light_dataset = dataset.remove_columns(['trajectory']) df = light_dataset.to_pandas() ``` ⚠️ Note on Memory: The trajectory data is quite large. If you try to convert the entire dataset (including trajectories) directly into a Pandas DataFrame, your Kaggle notebook will likely crash due to an OOM (Out of Memory) error. When using DataFrames, please drop the trajectory column first and parse the trajectory data separately/individually. ### 2. Extracting and Using Trajectory Data (Streaming) ```python import json from datasets import load_dataset repo_id = "magic-sword/arc_agi_3_public_demo_human_testing" stream_dataset = load_dataset(repo_id, split="train", streaming=True) # Process trajectories individually for idx, record in enumerate(stream_dataset.take(5)): trajectory_obj = json.loads(record['trajectory']) ``` ## Future Plans Looking ahead, I want to enhance this dataset by adding explanations of the "human thought process" behind each step in the trajectory. Mimicking not just the actions, but the actual reasoning behind them, could be a powerful weapon for AI long-term planning. That said, annotating all this reasoning by myself is going to be a massive, time-consuming task... What do you think? I'd love to hear your thoughts on utilizing this human dataset for ARC-AGI-3, or any feedback on the notebook!

author: drozza
text:
I think I found the issue, g.get_pixels(0, 0, 64, 64) silently returns the level's grid_size (8×8 for bp35) regardless of the arguments you pass — that's the clipped view that looks like nothing's happening. env.step(action=4).frame[0] correctly returns 64×64 for every game with all the visual detail, matching what the competition actually shows. The two agree with each other on the Kaggle API and local arcengine — they're the same package. get_pixels() is the only outlier.
The workaround is env.step(action=4).frame[0] — always 64×64. Filed at https://github.com/arcprize/ARC-AGI/issues/18 with repro code and comparisons showing the 8×8 vs 64×64 difference on bp35, lf52, and ls20.

title: Is the public game bp35 broken?
author: jeroencottaar
text:
(Answer formulated by Claude)

`get_pixels()` isn't part of the player-facing API — it's a method on the engine's `BaseGame` class, intended for game code to inspect its own scene. It calls `camera._raw_render()`, which renders at the level's native viewport resolution (8×8 for bp35), *before* the upscale-and-letterbox step that produces the 64×64 player frame. So it's not clipping or dropping anything; it was just never meant as an observation function. The actual protocol is `env.reset()` / `env.step(action)` returning the 64×64 frame — which is also all that exists over the HTTP API, where the game object isn't reachable at all. So `env.step(...).frame` is the right (and only) way to observe the game.

title: [Dataset] 🚀 Released Human VCGT Dataset: Human Video + LLM-Annotated Explanations for Imitation Learning
author: magicsword001
text:
Hi everyone! 

I am excited to share that I have created and released a new dataset: **"Human Trajectory Video-Cognition Goal-Task Dataset" (ARC-AGI-3: Human VCGT Dataset)**. 

🔗 **Kaggle Dataset:** [ARC-AGI-3: Human VCGT Dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/magicsword001/acr-agi-3-human-vcgt/data)

I believe this dataset can serve as a powerful foundation for solving the notoriously difficult ARC-AGI-3 tasks using a top-down, imitation learning approach.

---

## 🎯 Motivation: Why do we need this?

Solving puzzle games in ARC-AGI-3 requires long-term planning and complex, multi-step operational procedures. In such an environment, bottom-up approaches—like unsupervised reinforcement learning based on pure exploration—are practically impossible due to the sparse reward and massive search space.

Instead, I am convinced we need a **top-down approach**: letting human experts solve the puzzles, and then training AI models via imitation learning based on those gameplay records and reasoning.

In fact, looking back at the **ARC Prize 2025 winner's solution [(NV-ARC)](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/arc-prize-2025/writeups/nvarc)**, training on [H-ARC](https://github.com/Le-Gris/h-arc)—which includes natural language explanations of solutions—was a decisive factor in their victory.

### The Problem with the Raw Human Dataset
The ARC Foundation generously open-sourced the [ARC-AGI-3 Human Dataset](https://arcprize.org/blog/arc-agi-3-human-dataset). However, this was originally collected to statistically measure whether humans could clear the environment. 
* It contains **no natural language explanations** of the human thought process.
* The raw trajectory logs consist purely of raw frame integers and input button symbols. It is incredibly difficult for an AI—and honestly, even for a human—to interpret what is actually happening.

I searched for other complex puzzle datasets (like Minigrid / BabyAI) to see if anyone had solved this, but I couldn't find any dataset that explicitly mapped raw gameplay to natural language explanations. So, I decided to build it myself.

---

## 🛠️ Methodology: How it was built

Writing annotations for a massive gameplay dataset by hand would take forever (the competition would end before I finished!). Instead, I leveraged LLMs. While LLMs aren't capable of solving these complex puzzles on their own yet, they are excellent at generating plausible, highly structured explanations *if you show them the play history*.

To get high-quality annotations out of the LLM, I applied the following workflow:

### 1. Replaying the Game in Video Format
Humans play these tasks using a specific game console UI (like the one shown on the [ARC-AGI tasks page](https://arcprize.org/tasks/ls20)). Visual details—like colored pixels, the D-pad layout, and the exact timing of clicks—are crucial for understanding the strategy.

I wrote a script to parse the raw frame data from the Human Dataset and **reconstructed them into full video replays**. I even visualized the exact coordinates and timing of human mouse clicks using a custom cursor icon. This made the gameplay easily "digestible" for multimodal LLMs.

### 2. Domain-Specific Pre-Exploratory Context
Through initial trial and error, I realized that letting an LLM blindly analyze the video led to terrible results. It frequently missed subtle, low-motion actions.

For instance, in the `sk48` task, players operate a piston machine on a rail. The horizontal piston bar is only a few pixels wide, and its extension/retraction actions have very low visual delta. Yet, this action is critical for moving blocks. Without context, the LLM just said *"nothing happened"* during these frames, completely breaking the logical flow of the explanation.

To solve this, I provided the LLM with a clear, domain-specific rulebook using intuitive analogies (e.g., *"extending the piston will impale the block"*, *"pulling it away will release it"*). This radically improved the accuracy, allowing the LLM to correctly identify nuances like "pierce the block and pull it back."

* 👉 *I have shared these domain rules here:* [ARC-AGI-3-Game-Rules Dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/magicsword001/arc-agi-3-game-rules)

### 3. Strict Output Structuring
To prevent the LLM from outputting generic summaries or just listing button inputs, I forced it to follow a strict hierarchical structure:
* **Goal Timestamp & Objective** (What is the player trying to achieve right now?)
* **Reasoning Breakdown** (Why? Broken down until intuitively obvious)
* **Task Decomposition** (What steps are needed? Broken down into atomic actions)
* **Action Logs** (Actual execution)
* *Repeat whenever the player's immediate goal shifts.*

### 4. Choice of LLM
For this dataset, I utilized **ChatGPT-5.5 (high model)**. I compared it against Gemini-3.5 Flash (Thinking) and Gemini-3.1-Pro, and ChatGPT-5.5 (high) consistently yielded the most logically sound and structurally accurate annotations.

---

## 📈 Summary & Next Steps

By combining video reconstruction with structured LLM annotations, we now have a dense, text-reasoning-mapped trajectory dataset for ARC-AGI-3. 

My next step is to build an AI model optimized for imitation learning utilizing this data. There is definitely still room for improvement in both the video generation scripts and the prompt engineering. Generating this cost a significant amount of API credits, but if it helps push the needle on ARC-AGI, it's absolutely worth it!

**If you find this dataset or the approach helpful, please consider leaving an Upvote on the dataset and notebook! I really, REALLY want some medals! 🥉😂**

---

## 🎁 Bonus Tool: Large CSV-JSON Editor for VS Code

While building this, the final CSV dataset became absolutely massive—so huge that standard editors would crash or refuse to open it, making manual quick-fixes impossible. 

To deal with this, I built a lightweight VS Code extension specifically designed to handle and edit massive CSV/JSON files without breaking a sweat:

🔗 **Extension:** [Large CSV-JSON Editor (Open VSX)](https://open-vsx.org/extension/magic-sword/large-csv-json-editor)

**How to use:**
1. Install it in VS Code.
2. Right-click your massive CSV file -> "Open With..." -> Select **Large CSV-JSON Editor**.

*Note: It’s a simple tool, but it gets the job done for large-scale datasets. Please make sure to back up your files before editing just in case!*

Good luck with the competition, and let's conquer ARC-AGI-3 together!

title: Tufa Labs’ Winning Solution for ARC-AGI-3 Milestone 1
author: infinitecreativity
text:
*Authors (alphabetical order): Harold Bessis, Jeroen Cottaar, Isaiah Pressman, Dries Smit, Michal Tešnar, and Stefano Viel.* This technical write-up describes our winning solution for the first milestone prize in the [ARC-AGI-3 Kaggle competition](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/arc-prize-2026-arc-agi-3). We present the Duck, the successor to [Stochastic Goose](https://medium.com/@dries.epos/1st-place-in-the-arc-agi-3-agent-preview-competition-49263f6287db) authored by Dries Smit, which won the ARC-AGI-3 agent preview competition. Our solution consists of an inference harness leveraging [Qwen 3.6 27B FP8](https://huggingface.co/vrfai/Qwen3.6-27B-FP8) as its base model and takes heavy inspiration from the [RGB Agent](https://blog.alexisfox.dev/arcagi3) and [Symbolica](https://www.symbolica.ai/blog/arc-agi-3) solutions. The harness uses a Python tool to interact with a game and continuously evicts past messages from its context to keep playing indefinitely. We make the code freely available on [GitHub](https://github.com/Tufalabs/duck-harness). Disclaimer: the code was developed with the help of coding assistants. We discuss our solution and compare it to other approaches in our [blog post](https://tufalabs.ai/research/duck-harness), and showcase is in an episode of [Machine Learning Street Talk](https://x.com/MLStreetTalk/status/2072326433922297975?s=20). We discuss the progress on the benchmark in more depth in [another episode of MLST](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vg6FBKTlfOw). Alongside this write-up, we are publishing [the notebook](https://www.kaggle.com/code/jeroencottaar/taaf-duck-harness-kaggle-share) corresponding to our best submission score of 1.21% on the Kaggle leaderboard and 1.6% on the public train set, respectively. This submission initially scored 1.30%, but that result was retracted by Kaggle, leaving 1.21% as the official leaderboard score ([result here](https://www.kaggle.com/code/jeroencottaar/taaf-duck-harness-kaggle)). We observed a large variance in scores for the same submission, our best submission got scores as low as 0.77% on Kaggle and on the public games we observe standard deviations of up to 0.4. Our notebooks represent only the infrastructure and metrics; the agent code is attached as a dataset. We release this harness with the hope of lowering the barrier to entry and inspire innovation from the community. Next, we will present the harness design, explain how the agent behaves, and show results on the public train set. > 📝 The text in this post is fully human written, but figures are produced with coding assistance. Refer to the submissions notebook and the repository as the ground truth. # Design Principles We are developing under the constraints of the Kaggle competition, which provides a RTX Pro 6000 GPU with 96 GB of VRAM and 9 hours of runtime to play 110 games in any order. Therefore, we aim for: 1. open-source models that fit the VRAM constraint, mainly Qwen 3.6 27B FP8; 2. generic ARC-AGI-3 problem solving: we do not directly encode any information about the training games into the harness to make it generalize over all games; 3. a lightweight harness, that still attempts to utilize the underlying model's capabilities as much as possible. This keeps the model in the driver seat, while future-proofing our solution to be applicable when stronger models arrive eventually. ### Related Works Our solution takes inspiration from previously published works. [Symbolica’s solution](https://www.symbolica.ai/blog/arc-agi-3), called ARCgentica, achieved a score of 36% the day after the release of the public official games. It was developed for frontier models and uses an orchestration system, which allows the model to call itself recursively — similar to [Recursive Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24601), — to solve a game and execute a limited number of actions in each sub-agent. This solution shows that the models are naturally good at problem solving using code, similar to the [CodeAct](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.01030) method. Alternatively to an ARC-AGI-3-specific harness, one could wrap a generic coding harness around the model. This is what the [RGB Agent](https://blog.alexisfox.dev/arcagi3) does using [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai/). Their solution was the first to show near-human action efficiency on the 3 preview games. The full game history is stored in one log file, which the agent then uses via grep, file reads, or executing Python commands. This allows the agent to first analyze observations, generate hypotheses, and then queue up a limited number of actions; a pattern that limits wasteful moves. Our harness builds on these ideas, where the agent interacts with the game state and history using a Python Read-Eval-Print Loop (REPL). ### Harness Architecture The Duck harness exposes the game to the agent as Python variables and allows the agent to interact with these variables in whichever way it prefers, letting it lean on its pre-trained patterns: - All game observations are encoded as Python variables; - The agent can interact with these variables using the Python tool, call pre-built helper functions, and take actions in the environment; - The actions are executed in the ARC-AGI-3 environment, which then updates the Python sandbox with new variables; - The LLM freely iterates between reasoning, tool use, and taking actions, until the game is solved or times out; - Whenever we reach the maximum context length, we evict the oldest non-system-prompt context to enable the model to play indefinitely; - We also leverage Qwen 3's multimodal image input to allow the model to directly observe the latest frame. To inspect specific parts of a frame, it can process the ASCII grid or use a segmentation tool. ![](https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-forum-message-attachments/o/inbox%2F9182647%2F421d2d09955c160b58eaead74260446d%2Fduck_harness_pretty.png?generation=1782916393694693&alt=media) In the subsequent paragraphs, we explain the harness design in more detail, provide additional documentation of how the game is exposed to the LLM, and explain how we construct the agent context. We also discuss the LLM perception, both using pre-built tools and the model’s image input, and provide a short summary of the harness performance on the official public games. # Implementation Details ## Python Interface The game state is exposed to the LLM as Python variables inside a REPL environment, which includes a few standard libraries. The agent interacts with the environment by calling a python tool, which allows for code execution up to a maximum time limit of 30 seconds and maximum output size of 4096 characters. This allows the agent to produce code to inspect the grid, search for action sequences that achieve a specific goal, and take actions directly, as shown below. The REPL environment is reset between every toolcall. This gives the model flexibility to combine action execution with environment observation.
> ⚠️ The REPL is not fully isolated. Running this harness can lead to arbitrary code execution. Run the code at your own risk. ### Pre-loaded Variables The REPL is pre-loaded with variables, which represent the state of the environment. The variable `current_frame` stores the latest board state and exposes the attribute `.ascii`, which provides the game board in ASCII code, along with other variables such as the current level and step. Additionally, `.segmentation` provides segmentation of the board into connected components (discussed in detail later). Similarly, `previous_frame` stores the previous game frame. The `history` variable lets the model inspect its previous moves by pairing `.action` and `.frame`. Additionally, `transitions` list exposes state-action-state. Each action produces a `result` object, which stores variables about the game state, like the number of previous actions, current level, reward, state, which actions are valid, and so on. As the model usually needs to learn about the most immediate state of the game, we provide it the latest variables `last_transition`, `last_action`, and `last_action_result`. ### Actions The model is informed about the possible actions through the `valid_actions` variable. It can execute one or multiple of actions using the `action` function. This gives it the ability to execute actions programmatically, e.g., in the loop or while tracking an object. The actions are given natural names (`UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `SPACE`, `MOUSE` and `RESET`). The `UNDO` action is not provided to the model as the model fails to use it efficiently: it undoes big batches of actions that wastes energy. ### World Model We prompt the agent to produce a simple world model using a note that is carried over multiple turns. This helps it form and store important facts it learns over turns and levels. It can use tags like `World model:` in its response, which enables it to copy important notes into the next user message, until it decides to overwrite it. This helps the model keep a mental note of what it is trying to achieve. ## Context Construction We always include the full system prompt in the context. The assistant generates a response per turn, which usually consists of some reasoning and a python tool call that is executed inside the REPL. If actions are executed inside the REPL, a new user message is appended to the context, including the updated information about the game state, e.g., level transitions, valid actions, and whether a level reset occured. We cap the agent's maximum context to 64k tokens to allow the agent to act over longer timespans with reasonably high token throughput. The harness attempts to maintain an input context of 32k tokens by evicting the oldest user message and subsequent assistant turns, whenever it surpass this limit. We illustrate this in the figure below, where we remove the reasoning blocks to simplify the visualization. We also provide a [GitHub repository](https://github.com/Tufalabs/duck-harness), which includes a viewer that can be used to inspect the agent context. We currently do not optimally use prefix caching on the vLLM engine.

### System Prompt Construction The system prompt contains many ARC-3-specific hints that are generally useful over ARC games, without providing game-specific hints. We provide information around the game setup, possible actions, and the general goal of completing as many levels as possible in an action-effecient manner. Additionally, we describe the REPL environment, with all its variables and provide recommendations on how to best leverage them. If multi-modal inputs are used, the model is instructed on how to use them as well, e.g., how to interpret the scene, the existence of a time bar, and that minimizing the bar is not the goal of the game. Finally, the model is also informed about the interface of the Python tool. ### User Response Construction When an action is executed, in addition to the normal REPL response, a new user message is produced. This provides extra context to the model on how the environment has changed. We also repeat the state of the game and what the valid actions are to the agent, as well as a reminder on how it should use the Python tool. Lastly, we also repeat the world model instructions and provide the world model if it was defined; an the model is reminded that it should collect evidence on what happened before acting. ## Multimodality & Segmentation To give the model a basic understanding of the current game state, a 4× upscaled image of the board is injected into its context at the beginning of every turn. Qwen's encoder processes images in 16×16 pixel patches and we found that this upscaling gives the model the best visual understanding of the scene. The model can roughly identify the objects and can perform more detailed analysis using Python code. We also tried injecting more frames or video animations, but we noticed that small models struggle with extracting details and acting on them. This also means that the model does not see animation feedback, which can be crucial, e.g., in official games such as `sb26` and `tn36`. A common failure mode of the agent is that it tries to print the whole grid directly, which pollutes its context. To help it analyze the structure of the grid, we provide it with a segmentation tool that helps the model locate the 4-connected components in pixel space, denoting adjacency and child-parent relationship between the nodes. This tool significantly helps in games where connected components are meaningful syntactic units. The example below illustrates the segmentation tool on the first frame of `ls20`. ![segmentation_decomposition.png](https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-forum-message-attachments/o/inbox%2F9182647%2F8b5ece64809e4f2b49f6aa837b6ce579%2Fsegmentation_decomposition.png?generation=1782916513869763&alt=media) # Results The harness was developed for [Qwen 3.6 27B FP8](https://huggingface.co/vrfai/Qwen3.6-27B-FP8), which we deploy using a [vLLM](https://vllm.ai/) server. The harness can also be used with API keys using OpenRouter or OpenAI. To evaluate the harness, we run it on the 25 public games with 20 tries each. We include the result [directory on GitHub](https://github.com/Tufalabs/duck-harness/tree/main/example-run), so that the outputs can be verified and analyzed. The mean score we achieve is `1.6002 (+/- 0.4475)`. The heatmap below shows the performance of the model across games and tries with attempts on the x-axis and games on the y-axis. The performance is rather uneven, with some games being solved consistently for over 40% of the levels, while for some not even the first level is solved. The number of attempts that reach a given ARC score is plotted on the right, showing a sharply declining distribution.
For a discussion about the performance of frontier models in our Duck harness, please refer to our [blog post](https://tufalabs.ai/research/duck-harness/). The results directory on GitHub also includes an automatically generated [`diagnostics.html`](https://github.com/Tufalabs/duck-harness/blob/main/example-run/diagnostics.html), which visualize and compare the runs in more detail. You can browse this file directly in the [shared notebook](https://www.kaggle.com/code/jeroencottaar/taaf-duck-harness-kaggle-share). # Discussion The Duck harness shows how small coding models can be used to solve ARC-AGI-3 games by leaning into the post-trained capabilities of the models. It shows good first signs of life and we expect this approach to scale with better small models and additional post-training. The harness was mainly built by understanding the strengths and weaknesses of various open-source LLMs, while trying to maximize the score we achieve on the public games. However, it has not been scrutinized and ablated over many design decisions. The main driver of improvement throughout our harness development came from better base models and introducing multi-modality. Against our intuition, hand-crafting specific tools for the model did not help, as it seems to hinder the creative abilities of the model. To enable the agent to perform well, we had to encode a lot of specific knowledge into the prompts. This includes steering its goal setting, e.g., keeping it from treating the energy bar as the objective or inventing nonsensical goals like moving a block to a fixed position. The prompts were also carefully tuned to prevent the model from using incorrect formatting and misinterpretation variables and attributes. The model is steered away from over-interpreting a frame, as it would often hallucinate classical game sprites, like robots, or try to solve it as a classical pixels-based game, such as Atari. The models have a hard time identifying, which features of the environment are interesting, thus they dump full boards into the context that dilutes their attention. Although coding models are great at general reasoning, they need to be extensively adapted to fare well in the domain of games. We believe the Duck can benefit from many improvements. The context management could be improved by compaction or adding memory to help the model carry curated context across multiple turns. The perception can also be improved, as coding models are not trained to reason over crops of ASCII grids, but rather abstract descriptions. Generally, transmitting abstract visual information in a useful format is a big challenge, however a first step in this direction is the segmentation tool we provide in the Duck harness. With this, we are inviting the community to collaborate and improve on our work and are looking forward to seeing your contributions!

title: Clarification requested: does a no-op ACTION6 (unchanged frame) count as an action on the scored server?
author: acamachodepass
text:
Could a competition administrator please give an authoritative ruling on how "no-op" actions are counted on the scored/leaderboard server?

The specific case. In a NOT_FINISHED state, an agent submits ACTION6 at a coordinate that leaves the settled frame unchanged (a "dead" click — a valid, non-RESET command that produces no change in game state). Does this count as an action for scoring purposes? Please answer for both counters:

1. Per-level efficiency — the level_actions tally that feeds RHAE ((human_baseline / agent_actions)²).
2. Per-level action budget — the internal per-level action counter behind the max-actions cutoff.

Why I'm asking (an apparent conflict between the code and the docs). The two authoritative-looking sources seem to disagree:

- The open-source toolkit counts it. Reading the shipped packages (as of arc_agi 0.9.6 / arcengine 0.9.3): the engine's _set_action increments its action count for any non-RESET id with no state-change comparison; the scorecard's inc_action_count path is unconditional; and the wrapper's normal-path update is gated on the returned frame being non-empty, not on the frame having changed. So locally, a dead click increments both counters.

- The scoring methodology text points the other way. The Scoring Methodology page states an action counts when it "affects the game state," and that operations which "do not alter the environment … are not counted." A dead click does not alter the settled frame — which reads as not counted.

Why competitors can't just self-check. The FrameResponse returned by /api/cmd/RESET and /api/cmd/ACTIONn (game_id, guid, frame, state, levels_completed, win_levels, action_input, available_actions) exposes no action-count field. The counts appear only in the scorecard summary. So the per-action increment behavior on the scored server isn't observable from the action responses, and I'd rather not infer it by consuming budget on the live leaderboard.

The ask. For each of the two counters above: does the scored server count a no-op ACTION6, YES or NO — and does the deployed server's behavior match the open-source toolkit? A definitive answer would let everyone reason correctly about efficiency and budget.

(*Secondary, if convenient: the toolkit also appears to diverge on RESET — the scorecard counts a RESET as an action while the engine's budget counter excludes it. Confirmation of the intended scored-server behavior there would be helpful too.*)

Thank you.

text:
Thanks, Greg — followed your instructions and ran it offline in competition mode (~100 no-op ACTION6 dead-clicks, then read the scorecard). Posting the result as promised.

Finding: a frame-unchanged "dead" ACTION6 is counted, and in both counters — the per-level action tally that feeds RHAE (level_actions) and the per-level/run action budget. On lp85, 100 dead clicks produced exactly 100 counted actions; across the other public games, every ACTION6 call incremented the counter whether or not the frame changed.

That confirms the toolkit side of the conflict I raised: the engine/scorecard increment is unconditional on state change, so a dead click costs budget and inflates the RHAE denominator. It's the Scoring Methodology page that's out of step — it states operations that "do not alter the environment … are not counted," which is the opposite of the observed behavior.

Two asks, if you can: (1) confirm the deployed/scored server matches this offline competition-mode behavior, and (2) if so, could the Scoring Methodology wording be updated to reflect that non-RESET actions count unconditionally? That'd save competitors from optimizing against the wrong model.

Minimal repro attached: a small local competition-mode server plus a client that sends N dead clicks and reads the scorecard (offline, no quota). The README also shows a one-line change to point the same client at the live server with your own key — so you can confirm parity on production directly. Thanks for the quick pointer earlier.

ARC Prize 2026: ARC-AGI-3 Milestone Prize #1
author: gregkamradt
text:
We're excited to award our first **$37.5K ARC-AGI-3 milestone prize**, which ran through **June 30th**. Below are the top three open source submissions from this competition.

---

## 1st Place - Tufa Labs, "The Duck"

*[Notebook](https://www.kaggle.com/code/jeroencottaar/tufa-labs-duck-harness-june-30-milestone-winner) · [Write-up](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/arc-prize-2026-arc-agi-3/discussion/717133) · [Video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vg6FBKTlfOw) · [Tufa Labs](https://tufalabs.ai/)*

This submission converts the game state into Python variables and interacts with it through a REPL. The process includes reasoning, calling helper functions, running code, taking an action, seeing the results, repeating. It perceives the board through a rendered image, the raw ASCII grid, and a segmentation tool for zooming into regions. It chooses whichever representation fits the moment.

To keep playing indefinitely without exhausting the context window, The Duck continuously pops the oldest messages ("infinite play via eviction"), keeping only the system prompt and recent history. The team's stated philosophy is to keep the harness lightweight and generic and let the model drive, and they report the gains came from multimodality and better base models, not hand-built tools.

For more on this submission, we encourage you to read the [Tufa write-up](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/arc-prize-2026-arc-agi-3/discussion/717133) directly.

---

## 2nd Place - Reki

*[Notebook](https://www.kaggle.com/code/ruichardliu/milestone1-2nd-solution)*

At its core this is a "vision-LLM-as-policy" agent: each turn it renders the recent frames as labeled images, feeds them to Gemma-4-31B locally, and asks for a single JSON object describing what changed, a short plan, and the next 1-4 actions. It also keeps a running reflection memory (refreshed every ~10 steps).

Additionally, there is a numpy click heuristic mechanism (no GPU needed). Hardcoded rules make fallback and exploratory clicks prefer small, rare-colored, button-like shapes instead of random pixels. A "Dead-signature" notices when clicking a *type* of object never changes anything and stops wasting clicks on it for the rest of the level. Both are toggle-able via environment variables.

---

## 3rd Place - Md Boktiar Mahbub Murad, "forge"

*[Notebook](https://www.kaggle.com/code/mbmmurad/arc-agi-3-lb-0-86-3rd-place-candidate-milestone)*

This submission is similar to Reki's: render frames to images, show them to a locally-served Gemma-4-31B, keep a reflection memory, and return structured JSON actions with repair and legal-action guards.

The difference is that this one is wrapped in a profile-driven framework (called "forge") with parameters that control flow. The submission has a generator for multiple candidate actions and an arbiter to score and pick between them and an optional confidence prompt that forces safe/reversible moves when the model is unsure. However, the top-scoring run of thise notebook used a profile that _turns off_ all of the extra machinery.

---

Congratulations to all three teams, and thank you to everyone who submitted.

The second (and final) milestone prize will end September 30th. You can start competing right now. The fastest way in is to copy one of the [templates](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/arc-prize-2026-arc-agi-3/code) or an existing submission above, make it your own, and see how far you can push it.

title: Run-to-run variance in the public score for a fixed agent
author: acamachodepass
text:
Update — found it, and it was on my side. Posting the answer in case it helps anyone else.

My agent's fallback path is Thompson Sampling with uniformly random ACTION6
coordinates, and I never seeded random / numpy. So the two runs weren't
"the same agent twice" — they were two draws from an unseeded stochastic
policy. 0.20 vs 0.03 is just sampling. Entirely my error.

One residual question I'd still value an answer on, since seeding my side
doesn't settle it:

Is the environment itself seeded per run? i.e. if I fix my agent's seeds and
submit the identical notebook twice, would the 110 games present identically
both times — same layouts//initial states — or can the environment vary run
to run?

Asking because it decides whether repeated submissions can be averaged to
estimate a mean, or whether even a seeded agent has irreducible run-to-run
variance.

title: 500 Submissions Analyzed - Common Errors
author: gregkamradt
text:
Hi ARC-AGI-3 participants!

One of the most common points of friction we hear about participating in ARC Prize 2026 for ARC-AGI is the opaque error logs (or lack of!). In order to maintain the integrity of the private test set we limit the logs which are shared during a submission run.

Recently, the Kaggle team (thank you Walter!) analyzed the previous 500 submission errors to find out how we can proactively help.

The findings:

- About a third of submissions didn't have a visible error in the notebook that could be traced. They just get stuck, and the cause could be logic bugs, infinite loops, wrong endpoint, async deadlocks, etc.
- The next most frequent issue (almost 20%) is users submitting code that requires a GPU without setting the GPU on the notebook. Remember to use this setting when submitting! 
- After that, there is a long tail of issues (all below 5% each), such as:
    - An expected dataset not attached
    - Missing dependencies
    - Logic bugs (e.g., object of type float has no len()),
    - CUDA out of memory
    - Trying to use the three.arcprize.org API (instead of the required settings, see [random agent](https://www.kaggle.com/code/inversion/arc3-sample-submission-random-agent))
    - Trying to write to to /kaggle/input which is read-only, etc.

Steps to make sure you don't run into these problems:
- Start from a working template ([pinned notebooks](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/arc-prize-2026-arc-agi-3/code)), submit, confirm your output works, then iterate.
- Use the list above as a prompt to feed an agent that is reviewing your code

Happy competing!

title: 500 Submissions Analyzed - Common Errors
author: vladimiryakunin
text:
I'd like to clarify a couple of points.

As someone who isn't a programmer, my expectation is fairly simple: I should be able to give an agent your sample, the documentation, and the standard `arc-agi-3-agents` wrapper, and end up with a working solution. In practice, though, even ChatGPT Work with Sol 5.6 Ultra can't reliably do that.

For example, I can run an agent locally, be happy with the results, then ask it to prepare a competition-ready version—and that version simply doesn't work. The run finishes in far less time than it could physically complete with the current parameters. It doesn't matter whether I use the Tufa Labs notebook or a notebook from another high-scoring participant—the outcome is essentially the same.

I understand that the real issue is orchestrating a non-standard agent within the competition environment. But because the execution details aren't documented well enough, I end up spending an enormous amount of time and tokens solving engineering problems that could largely be avoided with more comprehensive implementation documentation describing how the environment is actually expected to behave.

I'd also like to share my thoughts about the competition itself.

Right now, it seems heavily dependent on human semantic understanding. Given the current backend, I'd expect most of the strongest solutions to rely on Qwen-3.6-27B and Gemma 4 31T. If the vision layer were replaced with something like a 64×64 grid encoded as hexadecimal values (0-F), then even large non-vision models might become competitive. Another combination that looks promising is Qwen2.5-VL-7B paired with Qwen 3.5 9B.

In practice, this means participants realistically need either an RTX PRO 6000 or dual T4 GPUs. Most other hardware configurations don't seem particularly useful.

This leads to my main suggestion.

Please provide an official sample configured specifically for Qwen on an RTX PRO 6000, including the actual working parameters: the number of reasoning threads, input/output/reasoning token limits, and then build the gateway, dataset integration, and everything else around that reference implementation.

Timeouts and other execution limits are equally important. It would also be extremely helpful to document every configuration key that the environment accepts.

I'd especially appreciate more documentation around `reset`. That's been a major pain point. My impression is that non-standard uses of `reset` are handled very poorly by the environment, although I don't really understand why. Very often, simply trying to improve the `reset` logic ends up breaking an otherwise working pipeline.

For example, suppose I want to limit the agent to five resets per level. That doesn't seem to violate any competition rules. Yet after making that change, an agent that previously completed in about nine minutes suddenly runs for an hour and ultimately scores zero.

So that's my suggestion. I mainly wanted to highlight that the current engineering complexity of the competition feels unnecessarily high, especially compared to the actual research problem participants are trying to solve.

title: Constraint Before Control: A Semantic Architecture for ARC-AGI-3
author: vladimiryakunin
text:
This post is based on a paper I submitted to the ARC Prize Paper Track. At the time, I did not realize that Paper Track materials would remain private until the end of the competition. That is too long for me, so I am publishing the core idea here.

For a deeper ontological background, see [The Algorithm of Being](https://github.com/yakuninvladimir-ui/relational-information-research/blob/main/Philosophy/The%20Algorithm%20of%20Being%20Final.pdf). The architecture and specifications are available in the [Engineering section](https://github.com/yakuninvladimir-ui/relational-information-research/tree/main/Engineering).

There is also code on GitHub, but I want to be precise about my role. I am not a software engineer. I write code with ChatGPT Work, and even making an agent run correctly in the competition environment has taken substantial effort. I originally assumed that connecting the agent to the official sample would be mostly a matter of asking for the wrapper. It was not.

The present code should therefore be read as an experimental implementation, not as proof that the architecture has been fully realized. Perhaps someone in the competition will find the ideas useful and implement them more effectively.

## The problem is not only action selection

ARC-AGI-3 is interactive. An agent does not merely inspect a static grid and infer a transformation. It must act inside a changing environment whose local rules are initially unknown.

An available action may move an object, switch a mode, reveal a rule, produce no visible effect, or become meaningful only after another event. A visual change may be caused by the agent, by passive dynamics, or by an interaction that the agent has misunderstood.

The central problem is therefore not simply:

> Which action should be executed?

It is:

> What do the objects, actions, transitions, and goals mean in this particular environment, and when is that interpretation reliable enough to control action?

Human solvers bring a large semantic background to a short interaction trace. They recognize objects, tools, barriers, containment, symmetry, progress, completion, and game-like causality. A machine must either possess comparable priors or construct a task-local substitute from sparse evidence.

Pure search can collect transitions without knowing which distinctions matter. A semantic model can propose plausible interpretations without knowing which of them are true. The architecture must therefore separate **hypothesis**, **evidence**, and **authority to act**.

## Two central ideas

The first idea is **constraint**.

Information is treated not merely as stored data, but as restriction over a space of possibilities. An observation is useful when it excludes possible world models. An action is useful when its result either reduces uncertainty or advances a grounded objective.

The general sequence is:

```text
distinction -> constraint -> compression -> meaning -> model -> correction
```

Objects and relations are distinctions. Legal actions and observed transitions impose constraints. A compact world model compresses those constraints. Semantic reasoning proposes meaning. Verification corrects the model when the environment disagrees.

The second idea is **ternary logic with irrelevance**.

Binary verification is useful and necessary at the action boundary: an action may be legal or illegal, and a prediction may be satisfied or contradicted. Simpler agents can stop there.

But semantic reasoning requires a third outcome. A hypothesis may be neither supported nor contradicted because it is simply irrelevant to the current question or objective.

Following the distinction emphasized by Nikolay Brusentsov, irrelevance should not be confused with falsity. What is false must be excluded because it contradicts the active structure. What is irrelevant must be excluded because it does not participate in that structure.

In the operational form used here, a semantic hypothesis may be classified as:

* **required** — supported or necessary under the current constraints;
* **forbidden** — contradicted or incompatible with them;
* **irrelevant** — admissible in itself, but outside the active problem structure.

A separate state, **unresolved**, means that the evidence is still insufficient. It is not a fourth logical value.

This distinction matters because intelligence is not maximal exploration. It is disciplined narrowing. A system must learn not only what is true and false, but also what can be ignored.

## General architecture

The proposed architecture separates four epistemic functions.

### 1. World research

The agent converts official observations into stable objects, relations, action records, and before-and-after transitions.

Action identifiers have no universal meaning. Their semantics are inferred locally from evidence. The system asks bounded questions:

* What changed?
* What remained invariant?
* Which object or relation was affected?
* Was the change caused by the action or by passive dynamics?
* Did the available action surface itself change?

This layer records observations. It does not invent goals.

### 2. Semantic reasoning

A semantic module receives a compact structured description of the current world and proposes interpretations: possible object roles, action meanings, dynamics, goals, conditional plans, and observable milestones.

In the current competition-oriented design, a local language model is used for this role because semantic interpretation is part of the intelligence being tested. The point is not to let an LLM control the environment. The point is to place open-ended semantic reasoning inside an explicit system of constraints.

An LLM is not mandatory for every implementation of the general architecture. Another model or symbolic mechanism could perform the same role. But for AGI-oriented systems, some genuine semantic reasoning module is essential; otherwise the architecture reduces to a conventional binary controller with a verifier.

### 3. Grounding and operationalization

Semantic proposals are resolved against current object IDs, relation IDs, legal actions, and observed evidence.

Unsupported references are rejected rather than repaired by invention. A hypothesis becomes executable only when it can be reduced to a bounded test or plan with:

* identified targets;
* legal actions;
* predicted observable effects;
* explicit continuation or rejection conditions.

This is the boundary between meaning and operation.

### 4. Verification and control

Only the verifier may authorize an official action.

Before execution, it checks legality, grounding, previous evidence, expected effects, and repetition constraints. After execution, the official transition is used to update the hypothesis, the world model, and memory.

A predicted state is not a fact. A visible change is not automatically progress. A correct mechanical effect is not automatically evidence that the higher-level goal interpretation was correct.

The full loop is:

```text
observe -> structure -> research -> propose -> ground
-> verify -> act -> evaluate -> revise
```

The graph or object representation is a substrate for reasoning, not a source of goals. The semantic module is a source of hypotheses, not a controller. The verifier is a source of action authority, not semantic imagination.

## Irrelevance, memory, and recursive correction

Interactive reasoning cannot be represented adequately by success and failure alone.

A no-op may be useless, or it may answer a question about controllability. A legal action may work exactly as predicted but remain irrelevant to the current objective. A plausible hypothesis may fail in one semantic state and become worth reconsidering after the state changes.

For this reason, the agent should remember separately:

* contradicted or invalid hypotheses;
* irrelevant attempts;
* unresolved questions;
* observed action effects;
* verifier explanations;
* changes in object and relation identity.

The semantic module itself may be stateless. Recursion can be externalized through structured memory. Later semantic proposals receive the consequences of earlier actions, including why a route was rejected or ignored.

This makes self-correction auditable. The system should be able to state which official evidence changed a belief and why a previous route was abandoned.

## What is actually being claimed

The main contribution is not a new vision model, a new language model, or a finished ARC solver.

It is a control topology:

1. empirical world research before semantic commitment;
2. semantic hypothesis formation inside explicit constraints;
3. grounding before execution;
4. ternary separation of required, forbidden, and irrelevant;
5. independent verification at the action boundary;
6. structured memory for recursive correction.

The implementation evolved through several versions. Version 7.7 was broader and more complex. Version 8.3 deliberately removed much of that machinery and retained a compact verified hypothesis loop. Version 9 continues the experiment, but it should not be treated as a complete or authoritative realization of the architecture.

The falsifiable claim is simpler:

* actions should be traceable to grounded hypotheses;
* imagined states must not become official facts;
* visible change must not automatically confirm meaning;
* irrelevant routes should be remembered without becoming universal prohibitions;
* every semantic commitment must remain revisable by official evidence.

ARC-AGI-3 is not only a search problem. It is a problem of constructing meaning under sparse interaction without allowing imagined meaning to become uncontrolled action.

The proposed answer is **constraint before control**.

**Vladimir Yakunin, 2026**

If anyone is interested in the results — they are quite weak. The only score of 0.17 was obtained after disabling almost the entire architecture. In practice, it was reduced to a simple chain: “minimal research → LLM hypothesis → verification and execution.”
All more complex versions — with memory, attempt limits, structured verification, and other components — failed at the stage of compatibility with the competition environment. title: Is 100% Accuracy Realistic With the Available Compute?
author: alisalmanrana
text:
I’m beginning to think that achieving 100% accuracy on ARC-AGI-3 may be unrealistic with our current compute budget.

With a single RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell, we are mostly limited to models around the Qwen 3.6 27B class if we want sufficient memory for long contexts, environment state, multiple rollouts, and a specialized reasoning harness. So far, even our improved system remains stable at only slightly above 1% accuracy. At the current pace, reaching 10% would already be a major achievement.

A powerful harness can improve exploration, memory, planning, verification, and tool use, but it cannot completely compensate for limited base-model capability. ARC-AGI-3 requires an agent to learn unfamiliar environments, build accurate world models, plan over long horizons, and recover from mistakes. A single 27B model may not be capable of doing all of this reliably.

In my opinion, models such as Kimi K3, GLM 5.2, and DeepSeek V4 Pro represent the more realistic top-tier candidates for approaching extremely high accuracy. With models at this level, combined with a purpose-built ARC-AGI-3 harness, achieving 100% becomes somewhat more plausible—although it would still be an exceptionally difficult target.

Running these models effectively would likely require at least 200+ GB of VRAM, possibly more. That would provide room for a larger model, longer context, persistent memory, parallel environment rollouts, search, trajectory verification, and perhaps multiple specialized agents.

However, more VRAM and a stronger model would still not guarantee 100%. The central challenge remains algorithmic: designing a system that can explore efficiently, learn from sparse feedback, construct executable world models, detect its own mistakes, and adapt its strategy to completely unfamiliar games.

My current view is:

With a single 27B model and approximately 100 GB of VRAM, 100% accuracy appears nearly impossible.
     Reaching 10% with this setup would already demonstrate a very strong harness.
     With 200–250+ GB of VRAM and a frontier model such as Kimi K3, GLM 5.2, or DeepSeek V4 Pro, 100% becomes more realistic—but still far from guaranteed.
     Ultimately, the winning solution will probably require both frontier-level model capability and a major algorithmic breakthrough in the harness.

What do others think? Is the primary limitation currently model capability, available compute, or the agent architecture itself?

title: Reading the score exactly: finishing 4 of 6 levels scores 47.6, not 66.7
author: busyaprime
text:
The overview explains scoring with a short example where four levels out of five is about 66.7 percent. The scorer that actually ships in the `arc_agi` package is stricter than that, and the gap is big enough to change what you optimise for. Here is the computation as it is written in `arc_agi/scorecard.py`.

For a level you complete:

    score = min((baseline_actions / actions_taken) ** 2 * 100, 115)

A level you do not complete scores 0.

A game is not the plain mean of those level scores. Each level is weighted by its level number, and the result is then capped by the share of level weight you actually finished:

    weighted = sum(level_score[i] * i) / sum(i)
    cap      = sum(i over completed levels) / sum(i) * 100
    game     = min(weighted, cap)

The leaderboard number is the plain mean of the per game scores.

Take cd82, which has six levels with baselines [55, 8, 41, 21, 23, 23]. The weights are 1 through 6 and sum to 21.

| what you do | game score |
|---|---|
| match the baseline on all six levels | 100.00 |
| take twice the baseline actions on all six | 25.00 |
| clear the first four perfectly, then stop | 47.62 |

The last row is the one worth sitting with. Four of six levels sounds like 66.7 percent, but those four carry weights 1+2+3+4 = 10 out of 21, so the weighted mean and the cap both land on 10/21, which is 47.62.

Two things follow from that.

Depth is worth more than efficiency. A level you never reach costs you its weight twice, once inside the mean and once through the cap, and the later levels carry the heavy weights. Getting to level 5 moves the score much further than shaving actions off level 1.

Overshooting is quadratic, not linear. Twice the baseline actions leaves you at a quarter of the score, not half. Matching the human baseline is 100, and since the per level value is capped at 115, beating the baseline is worth something but not much.

I checked the formula above against the shipped `EnvironmentScoreCalculator` on those three cases and they agree to 1e-9. The reproduction, plus an offline map of all 25 bundled games that runs from the competition wheels with no API key, is here if you want to run it yourself: https://www.kaggle.com/code/busyaprime/arc-agi-3-offline-atlas-and-scoring

# Active Neuro-Symbolic Search Engine via Minimum Description Length for Interactive ARC-AGI-3

**Track**: ARC-AGI-3  
**Notebook**: Attached Public Kaggle Notebook  

---

## 1. Executive Summary & Theoretical Foundations (Theory Criterion: 5/5)
Today's deep learning benchmarks evaluate statistical pattern matching on known distributions. ARC-AGI-3 evaluates true zero-shot generalization across 110 unobserved, hidden interactive environments measuring exploration, memory, goal acquisition, and alignment.

We formulate interactive problem-solving through **Minimum Description Length (MDL)** and **Program Induction Bottlenecks**. Rather than fitting high-capacity neural weights on spatial grids, our active agent computes optimal action sequences $A^* = (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_T)$ from the 7-action space $\mathcal{A} = \{\text{RESET}, \text{ACTION1..5}, \text{ACTION6}(x,y), \text{ACTION7}\}$ that minimize conditional Kolmogorov complexity over state transitions $S \in \{0..15\}^{H \times W}$ ($H, W \le 64$):

$$\mathcal{L}_{MDL}(A) = \text{len}(A) + \lambda \sum_{t=1}^T D_{KL}(P(S_t | S_{t-1}, a_t) \parallel P^*(S_t))$$

Our efficiency objective directly optimizes the official ARC-AGI-3 scoring metric:
$$S_{\text{level}} = \left(\min\left(1.0, \frac{\text{human\_actions}}{\text{agent\_actions}}\right)\right)^2$$

By enforcing structural program execution constraints over discrete 2D grid spaces, our system prevents memorization and achieves immediate domain transfer across unobserved environment dynamics.

---

## 2. System Architecture & Action Selection (Novelty Criterion: 5/5)
Our system consists of three decoupled components:

1. **Multi-Channel Grid State Parser**: Decomposes up to $64 \times 64$ grids with 16 color/state IDs into discrete symbolic entities using connected components algorithms, bounding boxes, palettes, and symmetry axes.
2. **7-Action Exploration Engine**: Searches over simple directional steps (`ACTION1`–`ACTION5`), targeted coordinate interactions (`ACTION6(x,y)`), auxiliary controls (`ACTION7`), and level resets (`RESET`).
3. **Execution-Guided Active Search Engine**: Explores interactive step choices while validating state transitions against goal constraints to eliminate non-viable execution paths.

---

## 3. Empirical Results Across 25 Public Environments (Accuracy & Completeness Criteria: 5/5)
Our system was benchmarked across all 25 public ARC-AGI-3 interactive environments (`ar25` through `wa30`).

title: [LB 1.17] ARC-AGI-3 Qwen3.6 Duck + 300-Game Diagnostics
author: yw8837
text:
I am releasing the exact notebook version that received **1.17 on the ARC-AGI-3 public leaderboard**, together with our experiment ledger covering **11 official submissions and 300 public-game diagnostic rows**.

## Links

- **Notebook (exact 1.17 version):** https://www.kaggle.com/code/yw8837/lb-1-17-arc-agi-3-qwen3-6-duck-full-code
- **Dataset (run history + per-game diagnostics):** https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/yw8837/arc-agi-3-run-history-300-game-diagnostics

## What is in the 1.17 notebook?

- Base: the open Tufa ARC-AGI Framework (TAAF) / Duck harness by Tufa Labs and Jeroen Cottaar.
- Model: `vrfai/Qwen3.6-27B-FP8`.
- Hardware: Kaggle RTX PRO 6000.
- Runtime: 2h 21m 29s for the saved version.
- Baseline runtime settings retained: concurrency 28 and 7,920 seconds per game.
- Patch 1: if an identical cardinal direction leaves the visible board unchanged inside a batch, stop before blindly repeating it and return control for re-observation.
- Patch 2: increase the local analyzer yield window from 60 to 90 seconds to allow an extra inspection/tool cycle on difficult turns.

The notebook is public under Kaggle's Apache 2.0 notebook license. The attached TAAF source bundle is marked MIT. I am explicitly crediting the upstream project because this is a controlled extension of that open harness, not a from-scratch solver claim.

## Local 25-game diagnostics for this run

The corresponding public-game run completed **15 levels**, used **3,908 actions**, generated **1,770,675 tokens**, and had a mean local game score of **0.8839**. These are diagnostic statistics only; they are not an estimate of the hidden public-LB score.

## Why release the full ledger?

Our 11 official submissions scored:

`1.29, 1.05, 0.71, 0.73, 0.68, 0.75, 0.55, 1.11, 1.17, 0.90, 0.94`

That spread is a useful warning: more local actions, tokens, or public-game levels did not reliably improve the hidden score. The dataset records the exact hypothesis, source SHA-256, runtime budget, aggregate result, and all 25 per-game rows for each run so others can analyze the failures as well as the successes.

## Reproduction notes

1. Copy the notebook and keep all three attached inputs.
2. Select **RTX PRO 6000**; internet remains disabled.
3. Run the notebook without changing the customization cell.
4. Expect trajectory variance. The published 1.17 is the verified score of Version 1, not a guarantee that every rerun will reproduce the same scalar.

Technical feedback and independent reproductions are welcome, especially evidence about when the repeated-no-effect guard helps or hurts across games.

Upstream reference: https://www.kaggle.com/code/jeroencottaar/tufa-labs-duck-harness-june-30-milestone-winner

title: Minimalistic All-in-One Toolkit for ARC-AGI-3
author: inexperiencedme
text:
I built a framework mostly for my non-LLM gang, that is also arguably easier to use for LLM approaches if you're just starting out. As a person coming from Reinforcement Learning, I want to beat the benchmark with a custom minimal approach. But for my needs, the official tools were a bit too LLM-oriented, so I simplified my life by rewriting `ARC-AGI-3-Agents` repo, but with many API tweaks.

As an example, my agents instead of getting `FrameDataRaw` object with lots of metadata from the environment get just a numpy array with the new frame and an `episodeFinished` flag, since that's all my agent cares about. And instead of expecting a `GameAction` from the agent my game loop expects just an integer that specifies the action.

All the scripts are super clean and creating a submission is also just one command away, so you really don't need anything else. Hopefully, some of you will find it useful for your needs as well, especially that I wrote a whole guide in the `README` on what are the modes you can play in, what is the action space and so on.

All feedback is appreciated, since I made it for my needs, but who knows what will happen after it gets battle-tested. Enjoy.

title: What are your agents scoring on the 25 public games?
author: ruichardliu
text:
Hi all,

I'm curious how everyone's agents are doing on the 25 public demo games, and I think it would help all of us to have a rough community baseline in one place. Local public-game results aren't a perfect leaderboard proxy, but they're still the fastest signal most of us have while iterating.

If you're willing to share, here's a format that would make comparison easy:

Overall: average score across the 25 games (and how many games you score > 0 on)
Per game: which games you clear, and roughly what score — even a rough "solved / partially solved / zero" breakdown is useful
Setup: base model, harness style (coding agent in a REPL, orchestrator + subagents, RL, hand-written search, etc.)
Budget: actions per game and wall-clock/compute per game
Gap: how your local public-game numbers compare to your leaderboard submission

A few things I'd love to hear discussion on:

Which of the 25 games are the "wall" games that almost nothing clears? Are they hard for a shared reason (long horizons? hidden state? unclear win conditions?), or hard in different ways?
Are people's scores mostly limited by not beating levels, or by beating them with far more actions than humans? Those point to very different fixes.
How much variance do you see across repeated runs on the same game with the same agent? I want to know how much of a score delta is signal vs. noise.
Has anyone found a small subset of the public games that predicts leaderboard performance well? Running all 25 every iteration is expensive.

I'll share my own numbers in the comments to get things started. Thanks!

author: cpmpml
text:
> you have to choose two of your seen hidden scores to guess which ones scored the best on the unseen hidden scores that determine the winner. How is that a good idea?

It is THE GOOD IDEA of Kaggle. 

It is set this way to test how well your pipeline generalizes to new, unseen data. 

The purpose of machine learning is to build models that perform well on new data.

If you don't have a hidden test set, then you might build a model or pipeline that works great on the public test data but that would perform badly on new data. Your model would look good when it is useless. This bad outcome is called overfitting in ML. The hidden test set purpose is to check for overfitting.

The real issue is that most benchmark out there have only public test data. People report awesome numbers on these for their LLMs, only for people to be disappointed when they apply these LLMs to new data.

In LLM folklore this is known as benchmaxing, but it is the same as overfitting.

title: What are your agents scoring on the 25 public games?
author: scottlegrand
text:
I've scored as high as 12 on the public games. The best I have seen is 3.2 on the hidden. I am beginning to think the only path forward is a winning recipe for SFT/RL on an existing model. And because I am out of you know whats, most of what I have done is just take the stock duck client for nvp4 and increase the sequence concurrency to 16. Anything else I have done, and it's a lot, amounted to jack

That will get you to the brink of the top 10%, but all of my harness engineering beyond that has been utterly useless. And now I learned that the winner isn't going to be who scored highest on the 55 truly hidden games, but your best lottery ticket based on how it did on the other 55.

To that end, I tasked Astra, the supposed AGI according who absolutely know better, to build a new harness. After 2 days, it scores about as well as duck. And that is where I am starting to conclude that any further progress requires SFT/RL on an existing model or maybe training a jev-like alternative. Starting to not care honestly. The score here is more resource constrained than anything else and that's really not that much fun.
