title: Paper Track team-up: I have a finished write-up but no leaderboard score
author: borro1980
text:
I'm looking for a team-up for the ARC Prize 2026 Paper Track, and I'd rather be
blunt about what I bring and what I don't.

**What I don't bring:** a competitive ARC-AGI-3 score. I'm at 0.79 from a single
submission — the Duck harness at `n_passes = 1`, which is the configuration my
experiment required, not one aimed at the leaderboard. You can see exactly where
that puts me on the board.

**What I bring:** a finished, pre-registered write-up that measures the
ARC-AGI-3 score instead of trying to beat it. It works from the 500 published
game-runs of the Milestone-1 harness — 25 games × 20 repetitions of one fixed
configuration, so the spread across them is pure repetition noise.

Three findings, so you can judge whether this is worth your time rather than
taking my word for it:

**1. The score is dominated by a binary term.** 84.7 % of the repetition variance
comes from "did the agent clear level *n* or not" (bootstrap 95 % CI [78.5,
91.1]); only 15.3 % comes from the efficiency term the formula spends most of its
complexity on. The mechanism is downstream cancellation in the sequential level
structure: failing early erases every later level at once, which turns a modest
per-level success probability into a heavy-tailed score.

**2. The variance is concentrated in almost nothing.** Two of the 25 public games
carry 65 % of the total variance — one game alone carries 49.8 % — while two
games contribute exactly zero. Half of all 500 runs score exactly 0; the mean is
1.60 and the maximum 25.33.

**3. `n_passes: 20` does not fit in a Kaggle notebook.** The harness ships with
that default. Measured on my own run — 25 games, one pass, single RTX 6000, GPU
saturated at 193 generated tokens/s throughout — one pass costs about 124 minutes
of play plus 8 minutes of model loading, with all 25 games running concurrently.
Against the 9-hour notebook limit that is roughly four passes, not twenty. The
published 500-run artefact was produced under a deployment config declaring two
B200s and a 13-hour window. If you have been reading the winner's configuration
as a recipe, it is a recipe for different hardware. (Measured under my settings;
a shorter per-game budget trades depth for passes, which is its own decision.)

There is more in the write-up — a significance analysis of the leaderboard's rank
structure against the correct null, and a pre-registered causal experiment on
disclosing the scoring function to the agent, reported as inconclusive because
that is what it is — but posting those details before the deadline would rather
defeat the point of entering.

**Why this has to be a merger.** The Paper Track rules require the write-up's team
to match the team that made the ARC-AGI-3 submission. A paper can only document a
score its own team achieved, so I cannot simply write about someone else's work.
The team merger deadline is 26 October.

**The arithmetic.** As of 5 August, 118 teams have entered the Paper Track;
2,065 are on the ARC-AGI-3 leaderboard. The final leaderboard prizes stop at
fifth place, so if you are outside the top five your score currently earns
nothing — while the Paper Track pays $75,000 across three places in a field one
twentieth the size. Most strong teams never write anything up.

**What it would cost you.** Kaggle allocates prizes in even shares among team
members unless the team unanimously agrees otherwise and notifies Kaggle before
payout, so the split is negotiable but even by default. And the write-up would
need substantial rework: the rubric asks how thoroughly the paper covers *your*
submission, and mine currently covers a measurement, not a solver. That is real
work and I would be the one doing it.

I am not going to pretend the odds are good. The rubric rewards leaderboard
accuracy and progress toward actually solving ARC, and a measurement paper is
weak on both. My own estimate is somewhere around one in three or four for a
top-three place as a merged team, against roughly one in twenty on my own —
judge that estimate yourself, I can show you how I got there.

If any of the three findings above were new to you, that is about the value I
would be bringing. Reply here if you want to talk.

title: Solved (sort of): "system error" persisted across 7 straight submissions, even reproducing the exact code from the only successful run — fix was a brand-new kernel
author: antoinemah
text:
Following up on the "500 Submissions Analyzed" post and Scott Le Grand's comment ("something early and bad is ending my runs with no way to find out") — I hit the same wall today and wanted to share the full elimination process plus what actually fixed it, since the ending was surprising.

Kernel: antoinemah/arc-agi-3-pathfinder-agent-submission (private)

Timeline:
- Version 1: goal-directed rule-based agent, MAX_ACTIONS=3000. Completed successfully, scored 0.00.
- Versions 2-8 (same kernel, iterating on the same agent): every single submission failed with the generic "A system error. Please try resubmitting to resolve the error and contact Kaggle Support if it persists." No traceback, no detail anywhere — the downloadable notebook log only ever shows the pre-execution "Save Version" commit step (pip install, %%writefile, notebook to HTML conversion), never anything from the actual gateway rerun.

What I ruled out along the way, each verified with a real submission on that same kernel:
1. Disk usage — the framework's Swarm hardcodes record=True for every game, writing full per-step session JSONL to disk. On heavy multi-frame games this reached ~1GB locally for a single game. Disabled recording for the scored rerun. Still failed.
2. A real logic bug — found and fixed a case where the agent's action-selection order let movement actions structurally starve out the click action (ACTION6) on click-only games. Verified locally before/after against the actual game. Still failed once genuinely included in what got pushed.
3. Unbounded memory — the base Agent class never prunes self.frames (retains full per-step history for the whole episode); every game's thread runs concurrently in the same process, multiplying this. Capped it via an append_frame override. Still failed.
4. Action budget / wall-clock time — cut MAX_ACTIONS 3000 to 500. Still failed.
5. Pulled the actual Version 1 source from Kaggle's kernel version history (website only — API/CLI has no way to fetch old versions) and rebuilt an agent functionally identical to the only-ever-successful run, plus the two verified-safe fixes above, with none of the newer logic. This still failed identically, on that kernel.

At that point every code-level explanation was exhausted, including reproducing the exact logic that had worked before. Setup/config (gateway wait, .env, OPERATION_MODE=online, etc.) was byte-identical to the pinned official sample throughout.

What actually fixed it: pushed the unmodified official pinned Random Agent sample as a brand-new kernel (different slug, never touched before). Submitted immediately — completed successfully, scored 0.14, first try. Then swapped in our real agent on that same new kernel — no code changes from what had been failing repeatedly on the old kernel.

So it looks like a kernel that's been iterated on many times (8 versions in our case) can end up in some bad state that makes every subsequent scored rerun fail with this generic error, independent of the code being submitted — while a fresh kernel with the exact same code works immediately. Structurally this feels similar to what Zhengxu Yu and Anmol Kumar described in the submission-limits thread.

One more thing worth flagging since it isn't documented anywhere I could find: submissions that end in SubmissionStatus.ERROR don't appear to count against the 1/day limit — we made 7 failed submissions and 1 successful one on the same kernel, all on the same calendar day, and only got blocked (immediate 400 on submit, before even queuing) right after the one that actually completed. That's good to know if you're debugging a similar issue and worried about burning your one shot for the day.

Hope this saves someone else the same afternoon. Happy to share the old kernel privately with a Kaggle team member if it'd help debug why it went bad.

title: Agent.MAX_ACTIONS defaults to 80, the loop takes 81, and the README never mentions it
author: maximolorenzoylosada
text:
I read the shipped ARC-AGI-3-Agents harness before writing an agent, and one thing in it seems worth surfacing because it will look like a policy failure when it isn't.

The base class carries a default action budget:

    class Agent(ABC):
        MAX_ACTIONS: int = 80  # to avoid looping forever if agent doesnt exit

and main() enforces it with:

    while (not self.is_done(self.frames, self.frames[-1])
           and self.action_counter <= self.MAX_ACTIONS):
        ...
        self.action_counter += 1

Two notes on that.

First, it is off by one relative to its name. action_counter starts at 0, the guard is <=, and the increment is at the end of the body, so the body runs for counter values 0 through 80 inclusive. That is 81 actions taken, not 80. I simulated the exact loop rather than reasoning about it, and it returns 81.

Second, and more usefully: it is not in the README. I searched the shipped 137-line README for MAX_ACTIONS, "action limit", "action budget" and "80 actions" and none of them appear. If you subclass Agent without overriding it, your agent stops mid-game after 81 actions and the symptom is an agent that just seems to give up.

It is clearly a default rather than a rule — the harness's own Playback agent sets MAX_ACTIONS = 1000000 — so overriding it on your subclass appears to be expected. I would still like confirmation from the organisers that raising it is in bounds for scoring, since I could not find that stated anywhere either.

One more thing from the README that will bite anyone following older material, since the failure mode is an AttributeError at runtime:

    frame.score      -> frame.levels_completed
    frame.win_score  -> frame.win_levels

Notebook with all of it quoted and computed in-cell from the shipped source, so it stays honest if the organisers change the file:
https://www.kaggle.com/code/maximolorenzoylosada/your-agent-stops-after-81-actions

No agent or strategy in there, just the harness read. If I have misread the loop semantics I would like to be corrected.

title: Write Up: Taaf Anim Agent
author: jakobbrggen
text:
Link to code: https://www.kaggle.com/code/jakobbrggen/taaf-anim-arc-agi-3-solver
Link to the original TAAF write-up: https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/arc-prize-2026-arc-agi-3/discussion/717133

## Idea

Our experiments over the last months showed mixed results. On the one hand the agent is very token efficient and the model cooperates better than we expected — when we give it a tool, it actually reaches for it on its own. On the other hand, because of its size and its limited reasoning capability compared to frontier models, it needs a lot of guidance, and it makes avoidable mistakes that cost actions.

So we focused on two things at once: giving the agent **more tools**, and adding **fixed restrictions** that keep it from burning actions on moves we already know are useless. Up to this point only two of our experiments really worked, which is why this write-up is short. We still have plenty of ideas left, and we will keep the comment section and the notebook updated whenever we find something that might move the community forward.

## Key elements

**1. A hard no-op guard.** The harness tracks every `(level, board state, action)` combination that has already been executed without changing the board. If the model tries the exact same action in the exact same state again, the harness blocks it before it reaches the environment and tells the model that this action was already proven ineffective here. The blocked action costs no action budget — only one LLM turn.

This one is small, and honestly our own measurements of it are weaker than we first thought. It looked like a solid ~12–20 % reduction in actions used, but we later realised that our runs are bound by the **wallclock limit**, not by the action budget: every run hits the time cap. Under a time cap, "fewer actions" can simply mean "each turn got more expensive", and a blocked action still costs a full LLM turn. So take that number with a grain of salt — we did.

**2. Giving the agent access to the animation frames between board states.** This is the bigger change and the one we think matters. Details below.

## Animation access

This was one of the experiments we had planned ever since Tufa Labs pointed out that their agent cannot perceive multi-frame animations. It turns out this isn't a limitation of the environment at all — the information is already there and simply gets dropped.

The ARC-AGI-3 API returns `frame` as an **array**, not a single grid. The docs are explicit about it: *"Multiple frames may be returned if the environment advances internally (e.g., animations) before settling."* On the engine side, `arcengine`'s `perform_action()` renders a frame after every internal `step()` and returns the whole list. TAAF even wraps it nicely — `GameState` exposes `frame` (the last one), `animation_frames` (everything except the last) and `all_frames`.

The catch: `animation_frames` and `all_frames` are **never called anywhere** in the harness. The only path a grid takes into the agent is `state.frame`, which is `raw.frame[-1]`. Everything in between is thrown away.

How much is "everything in between"? On the 25 public games, **13 produce multi-frame responses**. Two concrete examples:

- **sp80** — this is the clearest case. The build phase is single-frame, but `ACTION5` starts the pouring phase, and that returns **22 frames, all different, with 624 pixels that only ever exist mid-animation**.
- **bp35** — every single action returns an animation and some movements can not be understood without the animations.

Since this pattern shows up in over half the public games, we assumed it would show up in the private ones too.

### What we implemented

Three stages, all behind one feature flag:

1. **Compact metadata on every action, always on.** Each action result now carries an `animation` field: how many frames came back, how many of them were distinct, whether the final board is identical to the board before the action, and how many pixels were transient plus their bounding box. This costs a few dozen tokens and needs no cooperation from the model at all.
2. **An `animation()` tool the model can call.** It returns a compact diff timeline — one entry per distinct frame with the changed cells, identical consecutive frames collapsed. `animation(frame=k)` reads a single frame cropped to the transient region, `animation(action_num=n)` looks back at an earlier action. Full 64×64 frames are never returned; one alone would blow the tool response budget. Calling it costs no in-game action.
3. **A proactive hint.** When the model is stuck in a level and the animations there are diff-heavy, the harness suggests calling the tool.

Point 1 is the important one, because it is executive rather than advisory. Points 2 and 3 depend on the model playing along — which, to our surprise, it partly does.

### But there are downsides too

We want to be honest about these, because they are the reason our public-set A/B did **not** show a significant improvement (+1.4 % mean score, p = 0.92 over 6 games × 4 passes), even though the private set went well.

- **Tokens are the real currency, not actions.** Every run in both arms hits the 132-minute wallclock cap. Nothing ends because of an action limit and nothing ends in a win. That means any change that makes a turn more expensive directly buys you fewer moves. Our animation arm went from 384 to **449 tokens per action (+17 %)**, and the effect was mechanical: in every single game, more tokens per action meant fewer actions, and fewer tokens per action meant more. On one game we lost 54 % of our actions and gained 129 % token cost per action. If you add information to the context, budget for it in moves.
- **The model calls the tool, but mostly at the wrong moments.** It used the tool unprompted in 21 out of 24 runs, so the willingness is there. But of 181 calls across all games, only **2 landed on a genuinely informative animation**. Out of 96 large animation events in the data, it inspected 2.1 %. Two calls went to animations that had *zero* transient pixels — where the metadata already said there was nothing to see. Most calls cluster in the first few analysis steps, which looks like exploring a new tool rather than using it when needed.
- **Watch your sandbox timeout.** Our single most informative tool call of the whole run died in a 30-second Python timeout and returned nothing.
- **It does not help everywhere.** In games where the animation is pure movement interpolation, the in-between frames contain no information that isn't in the final frame, and you pay full price for them. Picking the right games matters more than we assumed — and measuring which games those are with a random-walk script does *not* predict what happens under a real agent. We were off by a factor of ten on one game in both directions.

## Conclusion and outlook

So this is a short write-up, and you might wonder why we bothered. The reason is that with the TAAF agent and the attached dataset it can be genuinely difficult to tell what a given variation changed, if anything at all — so we would rather say it out loud, including the parts that didn't work.

We also want to encourage everyone to share their thoughts and ideas even though this is a competition. At least in this Kaggle competition, we are nowhere near 100 % and the grand prize, so there is a lot more to gain from comparing notes than from sitting on them. We will keep the comments updated on what we try next — at least as long as we don't think we are going to win with it ;)

Feel free to ask anything in the comments.

title: Write Up: Taaf Anim Agent
author: xuanyangge
text:
Great write up! I observed something similar and the frames are important for Sol but seems to blow up the context window for Qwen.

To give some background, I saw this article https://vista-research.github.io/ which has a very simple prompt about vision-only approach but achieved 100% for claude/Sol. The main idea is to actually enlarge the 64x64 grid to 512x 512 and utilize the model's vision capability. (because the model is trained more with online images that are like 512x512, using a 64 x 64 usually results in model not able to get the details of the image) 

Overall it seems like the vision information help Qwen get to the intuition about the problem faster, for example, for ft09 it is able to reason that the bottom right is the target area immediately after seeing the image. However, compared to sol, qwen cannot accurately infer coordinates based on image and is also worse in reasoning. Likewise, for the animation toolkit, it is vital for sol for problem like tn36 (I run A/B test for sol with duck/vista as well) but for qwen the vista approach just does not work as well.

Looking at the traces of qwen in VISTA setup compared to sol, it feels to me qwen could just need some fine tuning to just be more accurate and reason a bit more, the initial intuition is there. Wondering what's your thoughts on doing SFT/GRPO on qwen?

text:

Several of our submissions show **Succeeded + Public Score 0.00**, but the submission logs look like **Phase A (Save Version / commit)** rather than a real **Phase B competition rerun**.

With only **1 submission/day**, this burns the daily quota without a real evaluation. Looking for confirmation whether this is expected, a known platform issue, or a mistake on our side.

## What we observe

1. **Submission runtime ~29 seconds**, then `NbConvertApp` finishes.
2. Logs contain:
   - `commit_selfcheck_partial … No module named 'agents'` (expected on commit)
   - **No** `gateway:8001`, **no** `python main.py`, **no** long agent run
3. Output `submission.parquet` is the **commit dummy**:
   - 1 row: `row_id=1_0`, `game_id=1`, `score=1`
4. Kernel listing shows **no `score:` badge** under the notebook (unlike notebooks that appear to have completed a real scored run).

   - Phase A: write dummy parquet when `KAGGLE_IS_COMPETITION_RERUN` is unset
   - Phase B: wait for gateway + `python main.py --agent myagent` when competition rerun is active

- `KAGGLE_KERNEL_RUN_TYPE='Interactive'`
- `ARC_PHASE_DECISION … is_comp=False`
- `ARC_PHASE_A_SKIP_MAIN`

- `arc-agi3-20260811-204100-c92phaseb` (new; Phase A banners verified; not intending to waste another submit until this is clarified)

title: Potential persistent memory issue with the Tufa Duck harness
author: iamjasonfeng
text:
The Tufa Duck harness only captures persistent memory updates from visible outputs, but the model might put the updates in hidden reasoning instead. This is exactly what happened when I ran an Arc3 online mode eval with DeepSeek V4 Flash. A significant portion of the updates were put in hidden reasoning and were never captured. Tufa's prompt does not explicitly tell the model to put the updates in visible output.

I made a version of the Tufa Duck notebook with visible updates: https://www.kaggle.com/code/iamjasonfeng/tufa-duck-visible-updates

title: All my submissions score 0.00 — even an exact copy of the official Random Agent sample
author: benedictehelfer
text:
Here's a reply for the second thread that pulls the first one in.

---

Your other thread has the stronger evidence. This one accidentally weakens it.

In the earlier post you reported ~29s runtime, a 1-row dummy parquet, and "no score badge on the kernel". Those three together are hard to explain innocently. That's the case worth pressing.

The Random Agent test, unfortunately, doesn't add to it — it subtracts. The official starter docs say the sample "picks random actions, a baseline that proves your pipeline works end-to-end," and under troubleshooting: "My local score is 0.0. That's expected for the random starter agent. Your job is to make it non-zero." Under RHAE, an unfinished level scores exactly 0, and a random policy essentially never clears one. So "a perfectly healthy Phase B running the sample agent produces 0.00." Anyone reading this thread will say that first, and they'll be right. The score is not the anomaly. The 29 seconds is.

"The one measurement that settles it, and it costs no submission"

Kernel runtime and "submission" runtime are different numbers in different places. Open the "Submissions tab of the competition", not the kernel page, and read the runtime against the scored entry.

- ~29s there → "Phase B genuinely did not run." You have a platform report, and it's clean.
- Hours there → Phase B ran; the short log you're reading is Save Version output, which is expected to have no gateway and no rerun flag, and the 0.00 comes from elsewhere.

Every log quoted across both threads is consistent with being the Save Version run. Close that ambiguity before pushing further, because it's the first thing a host will point at.

"Also worth eliminating on your side"

Does anything write `submission.parquet` "before" the Phase B branch? If the dummy is written unconditionally and Phase B only overwrites it on success, then "any" early Phase B failure leaves the dummy in place and scores 0.00 silently — Succeeded, no error, exactly what you describe. Write the dummy only when `is_comp=False`, and let Phase B fail loudly instead of falling through.

The `commit_selfcheck_partial … No module named 'agents'` line is probably harmless on commit, but if `agents` becomes importable only after a setup step that behaves differently in the rerun, Phase B dies early and you get the same signature.

"Your questions in this thread"

1. In a real Phase B, yes. But those logs generally aren't exposed, so their absence isn't proof.
2. Same answer — expected in Phase A, unknowable for Phase B from outside.
3. Can't confirm. Nothing public describes a per-account scoring fault.
4. Before spending a submission: check the submission runtime in the Submissions tab, confirm which `submission.parquet` you picked in the Output File dropdown (multiple parquets in `/kaggle/working` will silently score the wrong one), and confirm the submitted version is the version you think it is.

"One calibration point" so a non-zero result doesn't surprise you later: a large offline→online drop is common here, not necessarily a fault. Another participant reports 1.56 in local eval on 20 public games and 0.02–0.05 on Kaggle Phase B across roughly 15 submissions. A fully working pipeline can still land very near zero — which is exactly why runtime and the missing score badge are the evidence, and the score isn't.

title: Public vs. Private Discrepancy
author: nicholaspellegrin
text:
I know a few posts about this topic have already been made, but I wanted to share what I've been seeing and hopefully someone may have some advice for me.

So I tried running the Tufa Duck harness with qwen 3.8, and got local scores on the 25 public games of around 2.1%, with a public leaderboard score of around 1.4%. The public notebook shows a high score of 2.2% on the leaderboard. So I think the gap between 1.4% and 2.2% is likely just the randomness from the sampling.

I then tried out my own harness with qwen 3.8, and got local scores around 5.0-5.4%, but my public leaderboard score is still around 1.4%. I guess it's possible that I'm overfitting, but I don't have any game-specific directions for the 25 public games so I'm not sure where my overfitting could be coming from.

I understand that the public games are easier than the private games, but I would think that the drop between public and private would be relatively constant, right? So if Tufa goes from 2.1% -> 1.4%, then I would expect my harness that scores 5.4% locally to do much better than 1.4% on the leaderboard. 

I also understand that with the sampling mechanisms with qwen that some variance in score is expected, but I don't think sampling alone could explain the gap I'm seeing with my own harness. Is this just a case of overfitting, or is there potentially a submission bug in my code? Has anyone found any common bugs that could cause you to see larger gaps in public vs. private scores?

title: GPT-OSS-120B works on the RTX Pro 6000 — offline vLLM 0.19 config + a fix for harmony-parser 500s (8% of requests)
author: rngrng
text:
Ran openai/gpt-oss-120b end-to-end as an agent analyzer on the competition GPU today. Sharing the config that works and one vLLM bug you will hit, since most public setups here are Qwen-centric.

## Attachments (all public)

- **Model**: `danielhanchen/gpt-oss-120b` Kaggle Model (Transformers layout, MXFP4, 15 safetensors). Weights load at **65.96 GiB** — fits the RTX Pro 6000 with room for KV cache.
- **Wheelhouse**: `driessmit1/arc3-vllm-h100-wheelhouse-v3` (vllm 0.19.0 + torch 2.10.0 + flashinfer 0.6.6 — from Tufa Labs' open-sourced milestone release; the versions are known-good together, don't mix wheel sets).
- **Tiktoken encodings**: notebook output `philipvonderlind/vllm-deps`. gpt-oss is a harmony model and `openai-harmony` tries to *download* its tiktoken encodings at import — offline you must attach them and set:

```
TIKTOKEN_ENCODINGS_BASE=/kaggle/input/vllm-deps/tiktoken_encodings   # o200k_base + cl100k_base
HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1
TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE=1
```

## Serve flags — the diffs vs. a Qwen setup

```
--tool-call-parser openai        # reads tool calls from the harmony commentary channel
--kv-cache-dtype fp8             # keeps 64k context in budget
--max-model-len 65536
--enable-prefix-caching
```

Two things to *remove* from a Qwen config:

- **No `--reasoning-parser`.** gpt-oss goes through vLLM's native harmony path (`openai_gptoss` is engaged automatically). Pointing `qwen3` at it fails — the vocab has no `<think>` token.
- **No `--default-chat-template-kwargs '{"preserve_thinking": true}'`** — harmony handles reasoning channels itself. Also note vLLM prints: *"For gpt-oss, we ignore --enable-auto-tool-choice and always enable tool use."*

Healthy numbers for reference: model load ~74 s, KV cache 15.86 GiB = **462k tokens** at fp8, sustained **~830 tok/s** generation with 25 concurrent requests, ~90% prefix-cache hit rate in an agent loop.

## The bug: 8.1% of requests 500

vLLM 0.19.0's harmony output parser (`vllm/entrypoints/openai/parser/harmony_utils.py`, `parse_output_into_messages`) has **no error handling**. gpt-oss occasionally emits a malformed harmony continuation — an `<|end|>` not followed by `<|start|>`, or a hallucinated `<|start|>functions.python` tool-result turn — and `StreamableParser` raises `HarmonyError` straight out of the request handler. The client gets a 500 and your agent loses the whole turn. Measured **91 of 1,127 requests (8.1%)** on a 25-game run.

Since the wheelhouse installs into a writable `--target` dir, you can patch the installed file before starting the server:

```python
# in parse_output_into_messages: wrap the token loop
parser = get_streamable_parser_for_assistant()
for token_id in token_ids:
    try:
        parser.process(token_id)
    except Exception:
        # malformed harmony continuation: truncate here instead of 500ing.
        # you keep the reasoning + any tool call that already closed.
        break
return parser
```

Both non-streaming consumers (`parse_chat_output` and the openai tool parser's `extract_tool_calls`) route through this function, so one guard covers both. With the guard, those 8% of turns degrade to "shorter answer" instead of "lost turn".

One last thing: assert your GPU before any of this. Kaggle once handed the notebook a Tesla P100 and the failure showed up minutes later as an opaque install error. `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name --format=csv,noheader` at cell 1, compare against what you expect, die loudly.

title: Offline vLLM on Kaggle: the wheelhouse pattern, mount-path gotchas, and env vars that bite
author: rngrng
text:
Competition kernels run with no internet, and a working local-LLM setup is table stakes here. This is the checklist I wish I'd had — everything below was learned by burning GPU hours.

## 1. The wheelhouse pattern

`pip install vllm` is dead offline. Attach a dataset full of wheels plus a lock file, and install with the resolver fenced off the network:

```bash
python -m pip install \
  --no-index --find-links /kaggle/input/<your-wheelhouse> \
  --requirement /kaggle/input/<your-wheelhouse>/requirements.lock \
  --target /kaggle/working/vllm-site-packages \
  --only-binary :all: --no-compile --ignore-installed --no-warn-conflicts
```

Details that matter:

- `--target` into `/kaggle/working` keeps the base environment untouched (the harness and its deps keep working). Export `PYTHONPATH=/kaggle/working/vllm-site-packages` to every child process that needs vLLM.
- `--only-binary :all:` means a missing wheel fails in seconds instead of attempting a source build that dies after minutes.
- **Pin a known-good trio and don't mix wheel sets.** `vllm==0.19.0 + torch==2.10.0 + flashinfer==0.6.6` work together (that's the combination in the public `driessmit1/arc3-vllm-h100-wheelhouse-v3`, from Tufa Labs' open-sourced milestone setup). I tried combining wheels from two different public wheelhouses and got resolver conflicts — versions across wheelhouses are not interchangeable.
- Write a **stamp file** after a successful install (contents = the pinned versions) and check it plus a `python -c "import vllm, torch"` before reinstalling. In interactive sessions this turns every restart from a several-minute reinstall into a no-op.

## 2. Mount paths are not where you think

The same attachment can appear at different paths depending on how it was attached and when the kernel was created. Resolve all candidates instead of hardcoding one:

- Datasets: `/kaggle/input/<slug>` **or** `/kaggle/input/datasets/<owner>/<slug>`
- Notebook outputs: `/kaggle/input/<slug>` **or** `/kaggle/usr/lib/notebooks/<owner>/<slug>`
- Kaggle Models: `/kaggle/input/models/<owner>/<slug>/<framework>/<variation>/<version>`

Print an audit of what actually mounted as your first cell. A missing attachment found at second 5 costs nothing; found after the model loaded, it costs half an hour.

## 3. Verify the model attachment before installing anything

A Kaggle Model can attach partially or in an unexpected layout. Check the cheap invariants first — `config.json`, `tokenizer.json`, the safetensors index, and the **shard count** (e.g. `model-*-of-00014.safetensors` should glob to exactly the number the index says). Only then spend minutes on the wheelhouse install and model load.

## 4. Env vars that prevent weird failures

```
HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1  TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE=1   # fail fast instead of hanging on a download
USE_TF=0  TRANSFORMERS_NO_TF=1             # stop transformers importing TF (slow, can crash)
VLLM_NO_USAGE_STATS=1                      # no phone-home attempt
```

If you serve a harmony-family model (gpt-oss), also attach tiktoken encodings and set `TIKTOKEN_ENCODINGS_BASE` — `openai-harmony` downloads them at import otherwise, which offline means a crash.

## 5. Smoke-test the endpoint before starting the real run

Poll `GET /v1/models` until the server is up (with a hard timeout that dumps the server log tail), then send one tiny `chat/completions` request and print the answer. A server that comes up but can't complete a request is a real failure mode (wrong parser flags, wrong template kwargs), and you want it at minute 6, not inside your agent loop at minute 40.

title: Fail fast or lose hours: guard cells that protect your GPU quota
author: rngrng
text:
With weekly GPU quota and long agent runs, the expensive failure isn't the crash — it's the crash that happens **late**. A run that dies at minute 3 costs nothing; the same root cause surfacing at minute 90 costs a real slice of your week. Everything below is a guard that moved a failure from "late and opaque" to "immediate and named", from runs on this competition.

## 1. Assert the GPU you think you have

Kaggle once provisioned a Tesla P100 for a notebook configured for the RTX Pro 6000. The visible symptom was an unrelated-looking subprocess failure minutes later. Worse outcomes exist: on a smaller GPU a big model can get through minutes of loading before OOM. First cell:

```python
import subprocess
names = subprocess.run(
    ["nvidia-smi", "--query-gpu=name", "--format=csv,noheader"],
    capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.split("\n")
names = [n.strip() for n in names if n.strip()]
assert names and all("rtx pro 6000" in n.lower() for n in names), f"wrong GPU: {names}"
```

Adjust the expected substring per accelerator choice. Seconds to fail, and the error names the actual problem.

## 2. Audit every attachment before any expensive step

Attachments mount at different paths depending on type and how they were attached (`/kaggle/input/<slug>` vs `/kaggle/input/datasets/<owner>/<slug>`, models under `/kaggle/input/models/.../<version>`). Print what actually mounted, then assert the cheap invariants of each input: the wheelhouse's lock file exists, the model dir has `config.json` + `tokenizer.json` + the exact expected safetensors shard count. A partially-attached model that passes a naive `path.exists()` check will happily waste a full install-and-load cycle before failing.

## 3. Smoke-test the model server before the agent touches it

After starting vLLM: poll `/v1/models` with a hard timeout, and on timeout print the **tail of the server log** in the exception — the alternative is a run that "hangs" with the actual error buried in a file nobody looks at. Then one tiny completion request. Wrong parser/template flags produce a server that comes up healthy and fails on first use; catch that in a 5-second request, not inside the run.

## 4. Leave before the wall clock throws you out

If the kernel hits the hard runtime limit, it is killed and you lose the outputs — scorecards, transcripts, everything you'd use to debug. Compute a soft deadline at start (`hard_limit - buffer`, I use 10 minutes) and have the loop exit cleanly when it's reached. A partial run with artifacts beats a complete run with none.

## 5. Cache expensive setup across interactive restarts

Stamp-file your offline pip install (write pinned versions to a marker file after success, verify with an actual `import` check before trusting it). Interactive debugging means many restarts; this makes each one cost ~0 instead of minutes — which in practice means you actually restart when you should, instead of nursing a wedged session to protect a warm install.

None of this is clever. But each guard exists because its absence cost me a real chunk of quota, and at ~2 long runs per weekly budget, "fails in 10 seconds with the real reason" is worth more than any throughput optimization.

title: Are the 110 environments identically seeded across scored runs?
author: kolenkovskin
text:
Two host answers already cover part of this, so I am only asking about the piece that still looks open.

Already answered:

* "Submissions run on all 110 tasks." — inversion (Kaggle staff): https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/arc-prize-2026-arc-agi-3/discussion/684852
* "Yes, the submission plays both datasets" — Greg Kamradt: https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/arc-prize-2026-arc-agi-3/discussion/729985
* "No, a seed is used for each one ... there are stable seeds" — Greg Kamradt: https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/arc-prize-2026-arc-agi-3/discussion/694153 (with the black-noise animation in lf52-271a04aa noted there as the exception)

Still open, asked two months ago without a host reply: https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/arc-prize-2026-arc-agi-3/discussion/726552

1. Are those stable seeds identical across scored runs? If I fix every seed on my side and submit an identical notebook twice, do the 110 environments initialize to the same states both times?
2. Is the public/private split of the 110 fixed — the same 55 games behind the public leaderboard for every submission — or can it vary run to run?

Why it matters: with one submission per day, this decides whether a repeated submission is a repeated measurement of the same thing, so runs can be averaged, or a draw from a different sample. title: Open-sourcing winning-trajectory datasets + a LoRA for the duck harness (STaR fine-tuning)
author: justforgags
text:
Hey all — sharing some artifacts that might help others fine-tune agents on ARC-AGI-3.

We ran the open duck harness (TAAF, MIT) with Qwen3.6-27B, kept only the games the agent won (reached a level), and LoRA-SFT'd on those winning trajectories (STaR / reject-sampling). Behavior-cloning the agent's own successes gave us a real, measurable lift on the leaderboard.

Three CC0 datasets:
- [arc3-sft-trajectories](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/justforgags/arc3-sft-trajectories) — full level-completing trajectories in chat-JSONL (system → reasoning → Python tool-calls → results). Drop-in SFT data.
- [arc3-duck-lora-sft](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/justforgags/arc3-duck-lora-sft) — the pilot LoRA adapter (Qwen3.6, qwen3_5).
- [duck-eval-results](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/justforgags/duck-eval-results) — per-game offline benchmark logs.

A few gotchas that might save you time:
- Train assistant-tokens-only; the tool-calls are OpenAI-format, flatten before templating.
- It's a multimodal arch — merge/serve as Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration (a text-only save gets rejected by vLLM), and copy the processor configs into the merged checkpoint.
- Offline levels don't predict the leaderboard — only submit to measure.

Hope it helps someone climb. Happy to answer questions. 🦆

author: ataraxian
text: I used to believe that LORA was the trick and spent a lot of time on it, but the result only backfired on me. It could be a skill issue but I also read later that Chollet said something about 'the local 25 game is not meant to be used as training data because the 110 game set is unique and much harder'.![](https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-forum-message-attachments/o/inbox%2F3101419%2Ffc43aed9ff1d372092f5601818096fc1%2F2026-09-03%20-%2017_09_38%20-%20Francois%20Chollet%20on%20X_%20_Regular%20reminder%20--%20the%20set%20of%20public%20ARC%203%20games%20is%20called%20_demonstration%20set_%20not%20_eval%20set_%20nor%20_training%20set_.%20It%20is%20not%20meant%20to%20be%20used%20as%20training%20data%20and%20it%20is%20not%20meant%20to%20be%20used.png?generation=1788427178228225&alt=media)

title: Open-sourcing winning-trajectory datasets + a LoRA for the duck harness (STaR fine-tuning)
author: justforgags
text:
A useful distinction here is what you fine-tune on.

Chollet's caution is about the demonstration set as data — training a model to solve those 25 specific games. That absolutely overfits: the private eval is different and harder, so memorizing the demo games buys you nothing there.

But "LoRA" isn't one thing. What gave us a modest lift wasn't training on game solutions — it was behavior-cloning the harness's own winning trajectories (STaR / rejection sampling): keep only the runs where the agent actually cleared levels, and SFT on the process — how it wrote probes, used the segmentation, structured its reasoning and tool calls. You're teaching agentic skill, not the answer key.

Why we half-trust it: the gain showed up on the leaderboard (semi-private) score, not on the local demo games — base model vs. the same model with a trajectory-LoRA, same harness. So at least in our case it wasn't demo-set overfitting.

Big caveats, and they line up with your experience:

1. High variance — same recipe, different runs, scores swung a lot. Very easy to read noise as signal.
2. Naively scaling the data hurt — more trajectories at the same recipe made it worse. Curation > quantity.
3. Base-model-specific — an adapter that helps one model won't necessarily help a different/stronger one, so as the meta shifts to new bases, old adapters can stop paying off entirely.

So: training on demo solutions → yes, backfires. Behavior-cloning winning process → can help, but it's finicky, model-specific, and only the private/semi-private score can confirm it's real.

title: MULTIMODAL_UPSCALE: the writeup says 4 is best, the popular forks all run 8 — has anyone actually A/B'd it?
author: asanashirov
text:
Two published claims about the same knob point in opposite directions, and I
can't find anyone who has tested it. Posting my measurements in case they help,
and because I'd rather not burn a 9h submission finding out what someone already
knows.

## The contradiction

The Duck harness writeup ([discussion 717133](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/arc-prize-2026-arc-agi-3/discussion/717133))
says the authors tuned this and settled on 4x:

> a 4x upscaled image of the board is injected into its context at the beginning
> of every turn ... we found that this upscaling gives the model the best visual
> understanding of the scene

Meanwhile the widely-forked Qwen3.8 submission notebooks run `MULTIMODAL_UPSCALE
= 8`, and the change from 4 to 8 is documented there as the arm that moved the
score. I inherited 8 without questioning it.

Both can be true — the writeup tuned against Qwen 3.6, the forks run 3.8, and a
different vision encoder could prefer a different scale. But I can't find a
single posted A/B, and it isn't a cheap thing to test: more visual tokens per
frame means fewer actions inside the same per-game cap, so it trades perception
against depth rather than being a free win.

**Has anyone run 4 against 8 on the same model?** Even a rough public-set
comparison would be useful, with the caveat below.

## Why I'm asking instead of measuring

Because I no longer trust the instrument, and I'd rather say so than let someone
else repeat the detour.

I ran the same notebook twice over the 25 public games in a single job (50 runs,
two waves, 4h25m):

| | mean score over the 25 games |
|---|---|
| pass 0 | 2.85 |
| pass 1 | 4.75 |

**A spread of 1.90 on identical configuration.** Every prompt-level arm I have
tried moves the public score by well under a point, so all of my arm rankings
were inside the noise and none of them meant anything. The authors report the
same thing from their side — 1.6002 +/- 0.4475 over 25 games x 20 tries — and
Jeroen has said the leaderboard itself ranges 0.7 to 1.3 on unmodified reruns.

Two consequences I'd suggest to anyone else optimising here:

- **Cross-team comparison on the public set doesn't work.** My runs land at 3.48
  and 4.57; the public figures I can read out of other teams' kernel outputs are
  3.77 and 3.79. Those cannot order us, even where the leaderboard separates the
  same notebooks by 3x.
- **A single submission is evidence, not proof.** At ~9h per rerun against a 30h
  weekly quota, that's a brutal exchange rate, and it's why I'd rather ask.

(One useful side effect: pass 1 scoring *higher* than pass 0 rules out "the stack
degrades over a long multi-wave run", at least out to 4h25m.)

## Dead ends, so nobody repeats them

- **Chasing the public-to-leaderboard drop as if it were a bug.** It isn't —
  Greg confirmed in [discussion 703990](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/arc-prize-2026-arc-agi-3/discussion/703990)
  that the public demo games are easier by design than the semi-private set, and
  that a large drop is expected. The ratio between the two measures how much
  margin your agent has, not how much score survives the rerun.
- **Removing the self-imposed rerun deadline.** Some forks set
  `soft_end = notebook_start + (max_runtime_s - 900)` while upstream's
  `_soft_end_time` returns `None` when running as a submission. Removing it
  scored 1.33 against 1.66 for the otherwise identical config. No improvement.
- **Worrying that hidden baselines break scoring.** In submission mode
  `environment_info.baseline_actions` can come back empty and
  `base_actions_per_level` falls to `None`, which makes the harness's *own*
  `_compute_final_score()` return 0.0. That had me worried, but it's
  reporting-only — competition mode returns early through
  `competition_scorecard.finish_run()` and never consults it. Your Kaggle score
  is unaffected.

Happy to share the two-pass per-game breakdown if it's useful to anyone.

Thanks to Tufa Labs for open-sourcing the harness, and for a writeup honest
enough to include its own weak spots.

title: What Have You Tried So Far?
author: phuongncn
text:
Let's share some short but useful experiences—what worked, what didn't, and what we learned along the way. Hopefully, we can learn from each other, avoid repeating the same mistakes, and save some valuable time.

Of course, I understand that this is a competition, and everyone has the right to keep their own edge or secret sauce. But personally, I see this as a learning journey: **the more you give, the more you get back. Winning is just a consequence.** ^^

For example, look at **Team Tufa**. They shared an excellent solution during the Progress round, then got overtaken by quite a large margin afterward—and now they're back at the top of the leaderboard!

So, here's what I've tried and failed at so far. **What about you?**

### 1. Gemma 4 31B

It seems to be better than Qwen 3.6 27B at image recognition and understanding visual content, but it falls far behind when it comes to logic and coding.

### 2. Using a system decoder to simplify everything happening in the game

For example, automatically identifying objects, figuring out which objects can move, etc.

This makes it possible for smaller models like GPT-OSS 120B/20B to understand and play the game. However, they tend to fail by taking overly roundabout approaches, and the decoder can also introduce strong game-specific biases.

### 3. Splitting the LLM into different roles

I tried assigning different roles to different LLM calls:

* Observer
* Theory Generator
* Action Taker
* Advisor

They can critique and challenge each other, and the overall reasoning quality seems to improve. However, the downside is obvious: **5× the LLM calls and a lot more tokens burned.** 😅

### 4. Trying different model configurations

I experimented with different Qwen distilled models, Qwen Thinking Cap, and turning thinking on/off.

The results didn't change that much.

With thinking **off**, the model is much faster but tends to be careless. With thinking **on**, the code quality is better, but it becomes significantly slower.

### 5. Experimenting with different concurrency levels

I tried 8, 16, 24, etc.

It seems that going beyond **16 concurrent requests** hits a saturation point. Increasing concurrency doesn't really make things faster and sometimes even makes the overall system slower.

My guess is that the KV cache becomes heavy, while prefill and decode start interfering with each other.

### 6. Playing all the games myself and creating training data

I tried playing all the games manually (and won all 100%, of course), collecting the data, and then training an agent to learn from it.

Unfortunately, training the model took a lot of time, and the result wasn't really better than simply letting Qwen 3.8 27B or 3.8 Flash Next play by itself. 😅

### 7. Building a strategy library for common game types

The idea was to create a knowledge base of strategies for common types of games and put it in the prompt, so the agent could retrieve a relevant strategy when encountering a similar game.

The problem is that this can easily introduce **game-specific bias** and make the agent assume that a new game works like something it has seen before.

---

The more we share, the more we learn.

**So, what have you tried? What failed? What surprisingly worked?**

Even a small finding might save someone else hours of experiments.

Let's share and learn together! 🚀

title: What Have You Tried So Far?
author: rakbidb

title: What Have You Tried So Far?
author: phuongncn
text:
Thanks for sharing so enthusiastically and for all the great ideas! Regarding your questions:

1. I tried playing the perfect-win games, recording every step, and then training a kind of reward model to encourage the agent to follow the right approach in each situation. However, it ended up learning by imitation and could only play that specific game.

2. For the different roles, to save tokens I only pass the information that each role actually needs. For example, one role receives the image, while another has access to the history of previous steps. At one point, I had a 5-role flow that managed to win a few public games using reasoning only (no coding agent like Tufa), one step at a time. But it couldn't run on Kaggle because it made too many LLM calls and ran out of the time budget :))

Right now, I'm focusing on optimizing the time spent on LLM calls. Token is money, and it seems that using fewer tokens per step is actually more effective.

And you're absolutely right that it's very difficult to reproduce the Tufa-family notebooks because they run games in parallel, while the noise is almost random. I'm also looking for ways to reduce that randomness. Do you have any ideas on how we could tackle this?

title: What Have You Tried So Far?
author: rakbidb
text:
Yeah, I’ve been thinking about this too. My current suspicion is that a lot of the variance may come from request scheduling + continuous batching, not just sampling.

When games run in parallel, tiny timing differences can change which requests are batched together. In an interactive setting like ARC-AGI-3, even one slightly different token/action can change the next observation, and then the entire trajectory can diverge.

A few things I want to test:

1. Per-request deterministic seeds.
   Derive the seed from something like "(base_seed, game_id, level_id, step_id)" so concurrency does not change RNG consumption order.

2. Replay the exact same prompts at different concurrency levels.
   For example: "1, 4, 8, 16".
   If concurrency=1 is stable but higher concurrency starts diverging, that would strongly suggest the randomness is coming from the serving/batching layer.

3. Fixed or synchronized micro-batches.
   Instead of fully asynchronous execution, maybe process small groups of games in a stable order. It could be a useful trade-off between throughput and reproducibility.

4. Ablate MTP / speculative decoding.
   Just to isolate whether they contribute additional variance.

5. Measure variance, not only mean score.
   I’m starting to think the practical objective should be closer to:

$$
E[\text{score}] - \lambda \cdot \mathrm{Std}[\text{score}
]$$

because a slightly weaker but stable agent may be better than one that occasionally scores high but is very noisy.

So my working hypothesis is:

Parallelism may not be only an engineering optimization here. It can effectively change the policy trajectory.

I’ll probably start with the exact-prompt replay × concurrency experiment first. If identical prompts only diverge when batching changes, that would give us a much clearer direction for reducing the randomness.

Would be interesting to compare results if you try something similar 😅

text:
I have a theory. And it explains the public/hidden variance/divergence. I made changes to the harness that would have given more time to games that hit L2 or higher. It got me to ~13 (up from 7.6) on the public data, it works. But it was a slight digression on the hidden data. The best explanation I have for this is that if your solver is at ~3.5 or less, you're mostly not solving any level 2 or up of the hidden games. The arc people have said the hidden games are harder so we don't truly have any representative training data (beyond subsetting the hardest of the open 25). 

I am guessing going forward, I need to focus harness development on synthetic games designed to be "harder than the public games" in the remaining month and a half. And I'm sharing this because in the spirit of competition, it's about the only thing that makes any sense to me at this point.

title: Efficient skill acquisition in frontier LLMs
author: homoalways
text:
The core of ARC-AGI is to test and facilitate the development of efficient skill
acquisition in AI, which François Chollet believes is the core of intelligence.

Now GPT-6 reaches a basically perfect score in ARC-AGI-3 (99.9%), double the human average. It's even found to be more "efficient" than humans — requiring fewer attempts than most people before solving a problem.

But how should we interpret this? Many people just judge based on an overall final score, which I don't think is informative. Have you looked at the details in how LLMs approach ARC-AGI-3? Have you observed or built in "efficient skill acquisition" capabilities?

Chain of Thought Reinforcement Decoding
author: iamjasonfeng
text:
Paper: https://github.com/iamjasonfeng/CoTRD

Abstract

Chain-of-Thought Reinforcement Decoding (CoTRD) is one of my solutions for the ARC-AGI 3 Kaggle competition. CoTRD is a test-time decoding method designed to increase the influence of an agent's previous reasoning on its next response without weight updates, an external reward model, or a symbolic representation of the task. It measures how the model's output changes when its previous reasoning is removed, then uses that difference during decoding. This paper documents three implementations in the following order: CoTRD (Full CAD), CoTRD Enhanced, and CoTRD Standard. It merely documents CoTRD and does not present or compare scores.

title: We will not be open-sourcing for the second milestone prize
author: jeroencottaar
text:
**TLDR**: We, Tufa Labs, will not be sharing our solution on September 30 for the second milestone prize, since we worry it may not be possible to beat the best of 4000 copies of that solution. We still plan to release our final solution when the competition ends. We encourage other top teams to share their intentions ahead of the milestone as well.

On June 30, we open-sourced our duck harness, claiming the first ARC-AGI3 milestone prize. Apart from the prize itself, part of our motivation was that we believed this would increase the quality of the competition by providing everyone with a good baseline to build on. This has worked out well, with all high-scoring public notebooks now building on this harness. We were not worried that further improvement wasn't possible; we knew that our harness was just the beginning.

With the second milestone on September 30 coming up, we are faced with a similar choice. This time, however, it is not so obvious that big improvements are still possible in the limited time that remains. We worry that if we (or another top ranked team) share our solution there will be 4000 submissions copying this solution, with the winner simply being the luckiest. Minor improvements would not help you; your score would need to beat the best of 4000, and variance is high. This has happened before, such as in this year's AIMO competition.

So we've come to the conclusion that we will not be participating in the second milestone prize, and so will not open-source our solution. We remain fully committed to sharing our final solution when the competition ends.

We understand that other top teams may choose differently. Either way, we'd like to encourage all top teams to clarify their plans; this also helps lower-ranked teams to know whether to share or not.

text:
From Game Theory perspective I don't think it is worth it.

The team basically sacrifices $25k for a better chance of gaining $40k. Tufa still has competition-winning talents and resource levels (which then can further re-invests the $25k on if they feel they are in danger of losing the spot).

There is also the risk that other 18-score competitors will also share and take that $25k and bolster their own chance instead. So this only makes sense to do if Tufa is really certain that they have a further secret sauce, but not enough to the point breaking over the potential variance coming from introducing this solution. But that is further the case to just get the $25k.

title: Finetuning a model (SFT or RL) on the RTX 6000 Pro?
author: nicholaspellegrin
text:
I've been toying with the idea of finetuning a model (either through SFT or some form of RL), but I haven't decided on a recipe yet. Part of the reason I've been holding off on trying this is because I'm not sure how realistic it is to fine tune Qwen 3.8 Next Flash NVFP4 on an RTX 6000 Pro.

I know that the RTX Pro is more than capable of finetuning Qwen 3.8 27B, but the gap in capability between 27B and flash next is quite large in my experiments (And I don't want to spend too much time finetuning 27B just for it to reach parity with base flash-next).

Has anyone had success training Flash-Next on their RTX 6000 Pro, or is the only option if I want to pursue finetuning to switch back to a smaller model and hope I can push it past the base performance of flash-next? Or if teams have found success training Qwen Flash Next, did you need to rent out more compute from somewhere else, and would that have an impact on the eligibility on winning the competition (if the hosts find excessive external compute not being "fair" to other participants)?

Any advice would be appreciated, and I don't expect anyone to share their "secret sauce" training recipe, especially so close to Milestone #2 and competition end.

title: Finetuning a model (SFT or RL) on the RTX 6000 Pro?
author: blakewest
text:
I've definitely been doing SFT with the models. But not on RTX 6000 Pro. All on H200's. That said, I have tried a lot of different approaches and so far have not found any recipes that work. For others, I have tried...
* SFT, using the Qwen Max as a teacher and also Astra as a teacher. 
* I've trained on synthetic variants of LS20 and CD82 just to try and find a working recipe
* I've trained using just "stall" points (eg. loops or lives lost), and also on "periodic" trajectories (ie. every 10th move) where at those moments, you hand the Duck game state to the teacher, and ask the teacher to take a move and then SFT on that. 
* I've tried it with different learning rates.
* I tried with Qwen Flash - Next and with Qwen 3.8 27B.

No permutation of these has been able to make meaningful improvements. I'm pretty convinced that finetuning with Qwen Flash Next is very difficult because it's an MoE model. I think 27B is more plausible, but still haven't been able to pull it off. Would love any tips from others who've tried or had some success!

title: Finetuning a model (SFT or RL) on the RTX 6000 Pro?
author: cputer
text:
Thanks for sharing all of this, it's genuinely useful to see what didn't move the needle.

One caution on the teacher side: OpenAI's Terms of Use (effective Jan 1, 2026) list "Use Output to develop models that compete with OpenAI" as a prohibited use, so fine-tuning a model on Astra-generated moves is risky under their policy. It also gets awkward for prize eligibility, since winning solutions have to be open-sourced, and weights distilled from restricted outputs may not be cleanly releasable. Worth checking the terms of whichever teacher you use before building a training set on it.

title: P3.1: Perception-Augmented Duck — What Prompt Engineering Can and Cannot Buy on ARC-AGI-3
author: gedouluhui
text:
**Milestone #2 technical write-up · September 2026**
**Authors:** gedouluhui (Kaggle)
**Base harness:** [The Duck](https://tufalabs.ai/research/duck-harness/) by Tufa Labs (Milestone #1 winner), used unmodified except where stated
**Model:** Qwen3.8-27B FP8 (Kaggle Models mirror: `foysalemonshanto/qwen3-8-27b-fp8-repacked-v1`)
**Hidden-set score:** **1.43** (single-play competition evaluation)

---

## 1. What this is

The Duck harness (Tufa Labs) won Milestone #1 and was open-sourced with an invitation: "The harness can still benefit from many improvements, especially in context management and perception. With this, we are inviting the community to improve on our work."

We took that invitation literally. This submission keeps the Duck harness architecture intact — REPL coding agent, ephemeral `python` tool, image + text grid perception, automatic context eviction — and changes exactly four things, each validated or rejected by a controlled experiment on the 25 public games:

| Change | Verdict | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Model: Qwen3.6-27B FP8 → **Qwen3.8-27B FP8** | kept | hidden 1.12 (P1) with zero other changes |
| **Perception hints** (deterministic connected-component click candidates) | kept | public EV 2.81 (P2.1) |
| **Prompt patch**: true scoring formula + remaining-time budget line | kept | hidden 1.43 (P3.1), +28% over P1 |
| Context 32k → 64k + output cap | **rejected** | 1.20 — throughput collapse (§5.1) |
| Temperature 0.6 → 0.3 | **rejected** | 0.95 — exploration collapse (§5.2) |
| Archetype playbook in system prompt | **rejected** | 1.54 — below pre-registered line (§5.3) |

Everything below documents the measurements, including the failures. We believe the negative results are the most useful part for the community.

## 2. The scoring rule, reverse-engineered (transfers to every competitor)

The competition page does not publish the exact scoring formula. We reconstructed it from the harness source (`tufa-arc-agi-framework`) and confirmed it against per-level telemetry across four full runs:

- **Level score** = `min(115, (baseline_actions / your_actions)² × 100)`. Every action — ACTION1–7 and in-level RESET — costs +1. A solution twice as long as the human baseline scores ~4× less; brute force asymptotes to zero.
- **Game score** = `Σ (level_index × level_score) / Σ (level_index)` over all levels, i.e. later levels are worth more, and an unfinished game caps out at the completed fraction. For a 6-level game, level 1 alone is worth at most 100/21 ≈ 4.76; for a 9-level game, 100/45 ≈ 2.22.
- **Leaderboard score** = unweighted mean over games.
- **Competition mode is single-play**: one `play` call per game, no retries. There is no way to re-attempt a game for a luckier draw.

Verified examples from our run logs: `su15` 1/9 levels at level-score 100 → 2.22 exactly; `tu93` 69 actions vs baseline 19 → (19/69)² × 100 / 45 ≈ 0.17 exactly.

Two design consequences:

1. **Probing and execution draw from the same account.** Every exploratory action spends score. The optimal policy probes until the mechanic is identified, then commits to the shortest reliable path — which is exactly what our prompt patch tells the model (§4).
2. **One cracked level ≈ 2–5 leaderboard points per game; mean over 25 games means each newly-cracked game is worth ~0.1–0.2 final points.** There are no small wins: a game is either understood or worth zero.

## 3. Setup

- **Harness:** Duck harness (ARC3-Inference @ `aa69123`, TAAF @ `fe9f7c4`), run via its official Kaggle path: vLLM OpenAI server on 127.0.0.1, REPL tool `python`, multimodal frames at 256px, context window 32,768 tokens with oldest-message eviction, history 30 turns, T=0.6 / top-p 0.95 / top-k 20, per-game budget 132 min, total wallclock 9 h.
- **Model:** Qwen3.8-27B FP8 (~31 GB), single RTX PRO 6000 (96 GB). Measured serving throughput: ~283 tok/s decode at 4k context, ~30 tok/s at 32k (prefill-dominated), via vLLM 0.19.0 offline wheelhouse (`driessmit1/arc3-vllm-h100-wheelhouse-v3`).
- **Evaluation protocol (public set):** all 25 public games, one pass each, 3000 s/game cap, same harness deployment defaults. This differs from the Duck team's 20-tries-per-game protocol; our numbers are single-draw means and therefore noisier by design (§6).
- **Hidden set:** official Kaggle submission, single play per game, ~9 h run.

## 4. The two patches that survived

### 4.1 Perception hints (deterministic, grid-native)

The Duck's weakest point on click-games is perceptual: the model must translate a 64×64 image into click coordinates through text reasoning alone. We added a small deterministic module (`inference/agent/perception_hints.py`, ~120 LOC, no learned components): when the action space includes MOUSE clicks, the current grid is segmented into same-color connected components (4-connectivity), and the analyzer's context receives the top candidate click points (component centroids, sorted by salience) as structured text.

The model remains free to ignore the hints; we merely remove the perceptual bottleneck of "where are the objects". This mirrors how the harness already encodes the grid as Python variables — we extend the same idea to spatial affordances.

### 4.2 Prompt patch (two lines, both grounded in §2)

Appended to the game-overview addendum:

1. The true scoring rule, verbatim: *"Scoring punishes long solutions quadratically: each level scores roughly (baseline_actions / your_actions)^2 × 100, so a path twice as long as necessary scores about four times less. Think before acting, then commit to the shortest reliable sequence and batch confirmed steps in one `action(...)` call."*
2. Budget pacing: *"Action results report `time_remaining_seconds`. Use it to pace yourself: probe until the mechanic is understood, then execute decisively. When several distinct hypotheses have failed on a level, stop repeating near-identical attempts and change the hypothesis class instead."*

The first line converts an implicit rule into an explicit objective; the second attacks the observed failure mode of hypothesis fixation (repeating near-identical failed attempts until timeout).

## 5. The three patches that failed — and why we trust the failures

All three were evaluated with the identical protocol, and all three were removed after hitting **pre-registered** decision lines (decided before the run, not after seeing the score).

### 5.1 Context 32k → 64k + 4096-token output cap: 1.20 (P3.0)

Intuition: more history = better world models. Reality: sustained throughput dropped from ~283 to ~195 tok/s, and the per-request latency at long context made the analyzer effectively slower per *decision*, not just per token. One game (`bp35`) burned 28k tokens producing **zero actions** — a truncation disaster where the model's outputs never materialized into tool calls. Reverted; 64k on this GPU/model pair is permanently sealed for us.

### 5.2 Temperature 0.6 → 0.3: 0.95 (P3.2)

Intuition: lower temperature = more reliable action syntax. Reality: the number of games with any progress collapsed from 12 to 8. At T=0.3 the model commits to its first hypothesis and defends it; at T=0.6 it re-generates alternatives after failure. The exploration in the tail of the sampling distribution *is* the problem-solving capability here. Reverted to 0.6.

### 5.3 Archetype playbook in the system prompt: 1.54 (P3.3)

Intuition: telling the model to first classify the game (NAVIGATION / PATTERN-REPRODUCTION / PHYSICS / CLICK-MATCHING / HIDDEN-COUNTER) and follow a per-archetype playbook should reduce wandering. Reality: 1.54, below our pre-registered keep-line of 3.5. Post-hoc reading of transcripts suggests premature classification locked games into wrong archetypes ("premature commitment" again, one level up). Removed from the bundle; the public dataset version of this submission does not contain it.

A caveat we applied to ourselves: at 25 games × 1 pass, run-to-run σ ≈ 0.8–0.9 points, so a single run can only resolve effects larger than ~±1.5 points. The rejected changes were not merely below average — they were below the noise floor's lower edge, and each had a mechanism visible in the logs (throughput, exploration count, fixation), not just a number.

## 6. The lottery effect: what actually limits this approach

Across four healthy runs of the same configuration (P2.1/P3.1 family), per-game outcomes are wildly bimodal: 17 of 25 games have been cracked **at least once**, but only ~5–8 are cracked in any single run. The same game under the same config scored 27.78 (four levels) in one run and 2.78 (one level) in another (`sb26`).

The dominant variable is whether the model's *opening minutes* land on the right mechanic hypothesis. Once the world model is right, execution is efficient (our cracked levels routinely score 100, i.e. human-baseline efficiency); once it is wrong, no amount of in-run recovery helps within the time budget.

Because competition mode is single-play, we cannot reduce this variance by re-sampling games. Capability must come from the model itself. This observation motivates our next step (probing Qwen3.8-Flash-Next NVFP4: 125B MoE with 6B active parameters and native 262k context, which fits the RTX PRO 6000 only via FP4 + host-offloaded N-gram embeddings) and, longer-term, trajectory collection for LoRA fine-tuning on winning transcripts.

## 7. Results summary

| Evaluation | Score | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Hidden set, P1 (harness + model swap only) | 1.12 | baseline reproduction on newer model |
| **Hidden set, P3.1 (this submission)** | **1.43** | +28% over P1 |
| Public all-25, P2.1 (perception hints) | 2.81 | single pass per game |
| Public all-25, P3.1 ×3 runs | 1.88 / 3.03 / 1.19 | EV ≈ 2.0, noise band 1.2–3.0 |
| Duck harness reference (their protocol) | 1.60 ± 0.45 | 20 tries/game, Qwen3.6-27B, public set |

Efficiency where we win: cracked levels average ~90–100 level-score (human-baseline action efficiency). The gap to the leaderboard top is concentrated entirely in games where no level is cracked at all.

## 8. Reproduction

All artifacts are public:

- **This notebook** (open-source license): full run logic, all 25 public games, self-check lines that print the active patch state.
- **Dataset `gedouluhui/taaf-p3-bundle`**: the harness source snapshot with our patches applied. Diff against upstream is exactly: (a) `inference/agent/perception_hints.py` (new), (b) two prompt lines in `inference/agent/prompts.py`, (c) one ACTION7 label fix in `inference/agent/action_names.py`. No other changes.
- **Model**: Kaggle Models `foysalemonshanto/qwen3-8-27b-fp8-repacked-v1`.
- **Wheelhouse**: `driessmit1/arc3-vllm-h100-wheelhouse-v3` (vLLM 0.19.0, offline).

Run: attach dataset + model + wheelhouse, accelerator RTX PRO 6000, internet off, Run All. Public all-25 completes in ~1–1.5 h; the submission configuration uses the harness's 9 h deployment defaults.

## 9. Attribution & license

- The Duck harness and TAAF: © Tufa Labs (Bessis, Cottaar, Pressman, Smit, Tešnar, Viel), redistributed from their public Milestone #1 release under its original terms — see `LICENSES.md` in the dataset. Our work stands entirely on their architecture.
- Wheelhouse: © driessmit1 (Dries Smit), public Kaggle dataset.
- Qwen3.8-27B: © Alibaba Qwen team, open weights; Kaggle mirror by foysalemonshanto.
- **Our increments** (perception hints module, prompt lines, this write-up): CC0 1.0 — public domain, no rights reserved.

## 10. What we would try next (roadmap, honestly scoped)

1. **Stronger open weights in the same harness** (Flash-Next probe running at time of writing).
2. **Trajectory collection → LoRA SFT**: every run already produces full transcripts in `/kaggle/working`; harvesting winning trajectories across runs yields a domain SFT set. Realistic expectation: 1.5–2.5× on our current base, i.e. ~2.5–4 hidden — not parity with a privately-trained 18-point system.
3. **Variance reduction inside a single play**: the only legal way to fight the lottery effect is making the opening hypothesis better, not sampling more games.

We thank Tufa Labs for open-sourcing the harness and explicitly inviting improvements, and the ARC Prize team for a competition design that makes single-play action efficiency the honest metric it is.

---
**Artifacts:** notebook https://www.kaggle.com/code/gedouluhui/notebook7081a28e35 · dataset https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/gedouluhui/taaf-p3-bundle

title: Partial-reasoning supervision made our agent stop acting: "no tool call" collapse in a small fine-tune (offline observations)
author: wkdrbwnd1
text:
We fine-tuned a small adapter on our own agent trajectories so the model would keep its tool-use habits with a shorter system prompt. We tried a few ways of deciding which assistant tokens get loss, and one of them failed in a way we did not expect. Sharing in case it saves someone a run.

**Setup (kept general)**
- Training data: 31 agent trajectories from 20 public games (thinking + python tool calls).
- Evaluation: 5 public games that were NOT in the training data (lp85, r11l, sc25, sp80, su15), all run in parallel. Same harness and prompt for every variant. 1 run per config.
- Two supervision recipes compared here:
  - **weighted**: tool-call tokens at weight 1.0, every reasoning token at 0.3.
  - **labeled**: we read the reasoning and labeled each sentence as (a) about using the tool interface, (b) generic problem-solving method, or (c) game-specific commentary, with weights 1.0 / 0.3 / 0.1. Tool calls stay at 1.0. The idea was to keep the "how to use the tools" signal and drop game-specific memorization. In practice about 92% of reasoning tokens were game-specific, so most of the reasoning ended up at 0.1.

**Results, 7-hour budget per game**

| | lp85 | r11l | sc25 | sp80 | su15 | avg |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| weighted | 82.1 | 27.0 | 5.6 | 0.6 | 10.1 | 25.07 |
| labeled | 10.3 | 4.8 | 7.4 | 0.2 | 2.2 | 4.99 |

With a 1-hour budget (and a slightly different prompt), labeled was actually a bit ahead (10.83 vs 8.88). The two runs disagree on which recipe is better, which says a lot about single-run noise. The failure below, though, showed up in both.

**What went wrong with labeled**

It was not code errors. Tool errors were 2.8% of turns for labeled vs 4.9% for weighted. The difference was turns that ended without any tool call:

| 7h runs | turns | turns with no tool call | degenerate-reasoning turns* |
|---|---|---|---|
| weighted | 3,668 | 132 | 148 |
| labeled | 4,767 | 1,474 | 624 |

\*A line repeated 4+ times inside one reasoning block, or "Hmm" more than 25 times per 1,000 chars.

The clearest case is lp85 (labeled):
1. Turns 0–293 are normal. The model clears 3 levels, and every turn ends in a tool call.
2. At turn 294 (level 4), reasoning grows to ~14K chars and hits the generation length limit, so no tool call comes out.
3. From then on, every remaining turn (1,231 in a row, until the 7h budget ran out) is ~2K chars of reasoning followed by a normal `stop`, with an empty answer and no tool call.
4. Our harness answered each empty turn with the same "you have not acted yet" user prompt, so the model saw nearly the same context every time and never broke out.

r11l and sc25 show smaller versions of the same thing, and the 1-hour runs had it too (49 degenerate turns for labeled vs 6 for weighted). Two independent runs pointing the same way makes us think it is a property of the adapter, not bad luck.

**Our hypothesis (not verified)**

With most reasoning tokens at 0.1, the adapter gets very little signal about how a reasoning block should end and hand off to an action. The loss concentrates on the tool call itself. Uniform down-weighting (0.3 everywhere) keeps the full "think → stop thinking → act" sequence supervised. Once the model produces one turn with no action, that turn stays in the recent history, and it seems to imitate it.

**Takeaways for us**
- Choosing supervised tokens by what a sentence is about can break a pattern that is about how the text is structured (reasoning → action). If you mask or down-weight reasoning selectively, check the no-action rate, not just the score.
- Separately, the harness should tell the model plainly when its previous turn produced no action or got cut off. Re-sending the same prompt leaves it no way to notice.
- Unrelated side note: listing explicitly in the prompt which attributes the runtime objects expose cut "wrong attribute" errors from ~7–8% to ~2.5% of turns. But levels cleared in the first hour did not measurably change.

**Caveats**
One run per config, 5 games, offline only. For us, offline ranking has not reliably predicted the leaderboard.

Has anyone seen partial-reasoning supervision (or reasoning masking) lead to this kind of no-action collapse?

I think this is a textbook game-theory setup, and the hosts designed it this way on purpose.

The top places are very close. Whoever open-sources gets the milestone money, and gets competition along with it: everyone else starts building on their work. Whoever keeps it closed gets no milestone money, and still faces the same competition the moment someone else publishes. Staying closed doesn't protect you if another top team can open up anyway.
